8 Fascinating  
Facts About Coffee 
Many of us cherish our morning cup of coffee. 
The aroma rouses us from sleep and launches 
us into a more productive day. The taste is 
comforting and invigorating. We cradle the 
warm mug in our hands as though it were a 
treasure. But how much do we know about 
coffee? 
You might appreciate your coffee even more 
after learning these interesting tidbits about 
its history and benefits. 
1) The coffee bean is extracted from a 
red berry 
The coffee plant is a shrub or small tree 
that produces edible red fruit, called 
cherries. Each cherry contains two seeds – 
and it is these that become our esteemed 
coffee beans. The cherries are picked, 
dried, and peeled down to the green seed, 
which is then roasted at a temperature of 
500 degrees until it doubles in size. 
2) Goats discovered caffeine 
cherish = love with a lot of 
affection, as if it were very 
valuable 
aroma = smell (this word is 
used for a nice smell) 
rouses = wakes up or causes 
to be active 
invigorating = gives you 
energy and strength 
mug = a thick cup with a 
handle 
tidbits = tiny pieces of 
information or food 
shrub = a bush, a type of 
vegetation that grows low to 
the ground 
esteemed = respected 
roasted = cooked with dry 
heat (no water) 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Legend has it that the stimulant effects of 
caffeine were discovered by Ethiopian 
shepherds in the 9th century, after they 
witnessed their goats’ unusual hyperactivity 
following a binge on the coffee cherries. We 
can only assume that the goats later 
experienced a caffeine crash. 
3) It’s a hot commodity 
After oil, coffee is the second most traded 
product in the world, beating out agriculture, 
animal products, metals, precious metals, 
natural gas, and the combined categories of 
butter, orange juice, sugar, and cocoa.  
4) Coffee could kill you… 
There is a lethal dose of caffeine, and that 
dose is roughly 100 cups of coffee in a day. It 
is said that Voltaire, the French philosopher, 
drank fifty cups per day. That’s more than 
three times the amount consumed by U.S. 
President Teddy Roosevelt, who downed a 
gallon a day. 
5) …but it will more likely help you live 
longer 
There are many health perks to drinking 
coffee, which is full of antioxidants. Studies 
legend has it = according 
to legend (unconfirmed) 
shepherds = people who 
take care of sheep & goats 
witnessed = were present 
to observe 
crash = sudden loss of 
energy 
hot = (informal) currently 
popular and successful 
beating out = performing 
better than 
precious metals = gold 
and silver 
a lethal dose = an amount 
that could kill you 
roughly = approximately 
downed = (informal) 
drank 
a gallon = a unit of volume 
equal to 3.785 liters 
antioxidants = chemicals 
that are believed to 
protect the body’s cells 
from damage 
Vocabulary 


 
 
indicate that regular coffee drinkers are at 
lower risk for conditions including 
Parkinson’s disease, Type II Diabetes, Heart 
Disease, cirrhosis, and dementia. Coffee 
does the body good. 
6) Coffee assists in weight loss 
Not only does caffeine stimulate an increased 
metabolism for fat burning, it also triggers 
an adrenaline release and unbinds fatty acid 
from fat tissue, both of which heighten 
performance while exercising.  
7) Cold weather + Americans = Irish 
Coffee 
Irish coffee, the rich cocktail of coffee, brown 
sugar, whiskey, and cream, was created by an 
Irish airline in order to help American 
passengers warm up as they disembarked 
into Ireland’s chilly and damp weather.  
8) The effects of coffee are immediate 
You’ll experience a caffeine rush merely ten 
minutes after your first sip of coffee. That 
means the potential to feel restored, 
energized, and ready for the day. So, what are 
you waiting for? Drink up! 
cirrhosis = a disease of the 
liver 
dementia = loss of mental 
ability caused by old age or 
disease 
metabolism = the process 
of the body breaking down 
food and using it for energy 
unbinds = disconnects 
rich = when a food or drink 
is described as “rich,” it 
means it’s very full of flavor 
cocktail = a drink where 
alcohol is mixed with other 
ingredients 
disembarked = got off a 
boat or plane 
damp = slightly wet 
rush = a sudden intense 
sensation 
sip = small drink

9 Jobs that No Longer Exist 
Due to technological advances and shifts in 
societal practices, there are many jobs that, for 
better or worse, have either become impractical 
or fallen out of fashion. Here are a few of those 
forgotten career paths. 
Newspaper reader: Before the era of iPods and 
headphones, factory owners used to employ 
people to stand on a podium and recite from 
that day’s newspaper in order to entertain and 
inform their workers.  
Bowling alley pinsetter: Today, bowling alleys 
are equipped with machines to clear the lanes 
and reset the pins, but before this technology 
was available, alley owners employed individuals 
(usually young men or teenagers) to stand at the 
back of the lanes and line up the pins manually 
after they’d been knocked over.  
Milkman: The advent of supermarkets has made 
this job extinct. But up until the 1960’s, 
deliverymen dropped milk on your doorstep 
every morning and returned in the evenings to 
retrieve the bottles. Today, those bottles are 
considered vintage. 
shifts = changes 
for better or worse = the 
result might be good or 
bad 
podium = a raised 
platform for a speaker 
recite = read aloud or say 
something memorized 
pins = the white objects 
you try to knock down in 
the sport of bowling, by 
rolling the ball down the 
long strip of wood called 
the lane 
manually = by hand (not 
automatic or done with 
machines) 
extinct = no longer exists 
doorstep = the area right 
outside the door 
vintage = old, classic items 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Lamplighter:  Nowadays we can turn on the 
lights with the flick of a switch, timers, or even 
hand clapping – but it was once accomplished 
with matches, wicks, and a very long stick. Men 
used to patrol the roads to kindle—and later, 
extinguish—each streetlamp one by one so that 
pedestrians could see in the dark.  
Food Tester: We can thank the Food and Drug 
Administration for sparing us from this 
responsibility. Before standard regulations were 
in place, it was the job of a human tester to 
ensure that food was free of poison – whether 
intentional or unintentional – so that royalty, 
politicians, and the rich could safely consume 
their dinners.  
Knocker-up: Most of us now wake up to the 
electronic beeping of an alarm clock – but in the 
past, people were hired to knock on the windows 
of doctors, factory workers, market traders, 
drivers, mill workers, and other professions that 
required early rising. They carried long poles to 
reach the windows of customers on upper floors. 
But one burning question is – how did the 
knocker-ups manage to wake up on time? 
clapping = putting your 
hands together to make 
noise 
wick = the “string” inside a 
candle 
kindle = start a fire 
extinguish = put out a fire 
or light 
royalty = kings, queens, 
princes, princesses, etc. 
beeping = a short, 
repetitive sound: “beep 
beep beep” 
knock = hit (usually on a 
door, wall, or window) 
burning question = an 
important question or one 
characterized by intensity 
of desire to know the 
answer 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Lung: As you may have guessed, this job title isn’t 
literal. In an age when alchemists, or old-time 
chemists, worked over a fire, a “lung” was a servant 
hired to fan the flames to keep the blaze alive.   
Necessary Woman: Indoor plumbing was available 
to very few people until the second half of the 19th 
century. Before that time, people relieved 
themselves in chamber pots, or piss pots, and 
wealthy citizens were fortunate enough to hire 
necessary women to drain and clean those pots.   
Switchboard Operator: Switchboard operators 
worked for large companies that might experience a 
high volume of calls, like hospitals, hotels, or 
corporations. The operators sat in a line facing a wall 
of wires and buttons. They wore headphones and 
first answered the phone call, and then flipped a 
switch to transfer the call to the appropriate 
department. This position existed even up until the 
1980s, until being replaced by receptionists as well 
as automated answering services that are becoming 
more and more sophisticated. 
There’s no need to mourn the demise of these old-
fashioned careers, though, because new professions 
are being created all the time. Nowadays, you can be 
a social media consultant, app developer, or robotics 
technician – and even more careers are bound to emerge in the years ahead!

of work

transmit electricity

complex

lessons.fullText:
Amazing Celebrations  
Around the World 
Cultures around the globe share a love of 
celebration. The reasons and methods for 
festivals are as distinct as the people 
themselves, and each one contributes to 
the rich heritage of human existence. Here 
are a few celebrations that stand out. 
 
Carnival in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 
 
This festival, which dates back to 1723, 
has become a world-renowned 
celebration. In its early days, rowdy 
celebrants took to the streets and soaked 
each other with buckets of water and 
limes – a tradition that often led to brawls. 
In the 19th century, the festival evolved to 
include parades with masks and music.  
 
Nowadays, over two million people flood 
the streets of Rio de Janeiro to participate 
in the singing and dancing, with costumes, 
ornately-decorated floats and general 
revelry.   
 
Samba schools from all over Brazil put on 
magnificent performances, each one 
relating a different story or theme. The 
beat of the music fills the air and you can 
feast your eyes on the vibrant colors and 
sights. 
world-renowned = widely known; 
famous 
soaked = made completely wet 
brawls = fights 
evolved = changed and developed 
parades = organized processions 
of people down the street 
flood the streets = completely fill 
the streets 
ornately-decorated = elaborately 
decorated, very fancy with lots of 
details

celebration

pleasure at 
vibrant = bright and intense 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
The Chinese New Year 
 
China commemorates the dawning of the New 
Year on a different schedule than the Western 
world, and its people don’t hold back in 
celebrating it. The Chinese New Year is the 
largest and longest festival in the country, 
with festivities typically lasting two full weeks. 
It is also celebrated in countries with sizable 
populations of Chinese immigrants. 
 
The celebration, which was traditionally a 
time to honor deities and ancestors, is 
replete with fireworks, lanterns and music. 
Families perform a thorough house cleaning 
to get rid of any bad luck and make way for a 
happy and prosperous year.  
 
South Korea’s Boryeong  
Mud Festival 
 
This rather odd tradition is a recent invention 
– it began in 1996 when a local cosmetics 
company created a line of mud-based beauty 
products. While most companies would invest 
in marketing and commercials, this one 
instead started the mud festival as a real-life 
example of the products.  
 
Attendees can participate in mud slides, mud 
wrestling, and even mud skiing. The event 
spread by word of mouth and became an 
international phenomenon – now millions of 
people come to the city in order to slather 
themselves in the mineral-rich mud. 
dawning = beginning 
don’t hold back = don’t limit 
or restrain themselves 
sizable = of significant size; 
large

family who have previously 
died 
is replete with = is totally full 
of; there are a lot of

protective or decorative case

attend something

telling other people about it 
phenomenon = incident 
(especially an unusual one) 
slather = cover completely  
Vocabulary 


 
 
Harbin Ice and Snow Festival - 
Harbin, China 
 
Each year in Harbin, China there is a truly magical 
celebration that blends art and ice. Craftsmen 
from around the country go to Harbin to create 
some of the most exquisite snow and ice 
sculptures found anywhere in the world. The 
exhibitions often include lasers and lights to add 
some special effects. Weather-permitting, the 
artistic creations last for an entire month.  
 
St. Petersburg, Russia: White Nights 
Festival 
 
The White Nights Festival is considered one of the 
finest international arts festivals. It takes place 
over the summer, the “season of the midnight sun” 
in Russia – hence the name. Created in 1993 to 
serve as “a musical gift to the city,” it features 
outstanding performers in genres ranging from 
opera to popular music to classical ballet.  
 
The culmination of the festival, which is called 
the Scarlet Sails festival, is a massive event 
attended by over a million people. Many of them 
are students and schoolchildren, as the event 
coincides with the end of the school year.

• Top 10 celebrations

Amelia Earhart: 
America’s Pioneering 
Female Pilot 
Amelia Earhart, one of the world’s earliest 
female pilots, was a trailblazer. Her legacy 
endures in the American consciousness today as 
a symbol of perseverance and bravery. 
Her aviation records were numerous; however 
she is most famous for being the first woman to 
fly across the Atlantic as a co-pilot in 1928. She 
then flew solo across the Atlantic again in 1932, 
once again the first woman to do so. She had 
strong convictions that men and women were 
equal in “jobs requiring intelligence, 
coordination, speed, coolness, and willpower.” 
Amelia was born in Kansas in 1897. She was a 
tomboy and seemed to have an innate spirit of 
adventure, enjoying outdoor activities such as 
climbing trees, collecting insects, and sledding.  
When she was eight years old, she cobbled 
together a ramp on the roof of a shed, then 
sledded off it into the air. Her “flight” and 
subsequent crash landing resulted in bumps 
and bruises, but she was exhilarated with the 
sensation of flying.

one of the first to do 
something, thus opening the 
path for others to follow

society

acting rationally

Vocabulary 


 
 
Amelia had enrolled as a pre-med student at 
Colombia University, but a year later, a 10-minute 
plane ride at a Long Beach air show kindled her 
love for aviation. She emerged from the plane with 
an unwavering determination to learn how to fly.  
Amelia went through a string of jobs, including 
schoolteacher, social worker, and photographer, in 
order to scrape together $1,000 for flying lessons. 
She cropped her hair short and wore leather 
jackets as she emulated pilots she respected. 
After six months, Amelia purchased a bright yellow, 
second-hand biplane. This plane, nicknamed ‘The 
Canary’, was the vehicle for Amelia’s first world 
record. In October 1922, she flew it to an altitude 
of 14,000 feet – the highest ever for a female pilot 
at the time.  
In April 1928, Amelia received an unexpected 
phone call from the organizers of the first trans-
Atlantic flight. They invited her to participate, 
thinking that having a woman on board would 
generate positive public interest. Naturally, she 
accepted the offer – but she was actually not 
allowed to fly, as it was deemed too dangerous for 
a woman to do so. This was a huge disappointment 
to Amelia, who later confided that she felt like she 
“was just baggage, like a sack of potatoes.”

studying to be a doctor

come alive

changing her mind

someone trusted 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Nevertheless, being on that flight opened up 
many doors for Amelia, and she received a 
rousing welcome upon her return to the United 
States. Dubbed “Lady Lindy”, she quickly became a 
spokeswoman for aviation. A publicist named 
George Putnam molded Amelia’s public image, 
and they worked closely during Amelia’s 
appearances and promotions. One thing led to 
another, and the pair got married in 1931. Intent 
on retaining her independence, Amelia referred 
to the marriage as a partnership with ‘dual control’ 
and made a point of keeping her own last name.  
Amelia went on to set many altitude, speed and 
distance records, as well as being a key figure in 
forming the Ninety Nines, a now iconic women’s 
aviation club. She also had a hand in promoting 
clothing and fashion that encouraged women to 
live a more active lifestyle. Amelia befriended 
First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt, who shared her 
passion for women’s causes. 
In 1937, Amelia set off on what was to become her 
final flight. She was attempting to circumnavigate 
the globe at the equator together with navigator 
Fred Noonan. With 22,000 miles down and 7,000 
to go, one of the last legs of the journey was from 
New Guinea to Howland Island – a small sliver of 
land in the Pacific Ocean.

The weather was overcast that day, and a ship from 
the U.S. Coast Guard was in the vicinity to help 
Amelia’s plane navigate. However, they were unable

of the ship’s radio system and the airplane’s radio

follow, Amelia was unable to locate Howland Island, 
and one of her last transmissions stated that her 
fuel was running low. 
Despite a massive search, no evidence of Amelia or 
her plane was found, leading to incessant 
speculation about her fate. Quite recently, a piece of 
wreckage recovered from a nearby uninhabited 
island has been identified as a potential piece of the 
plane. It is possible that Amelia and her navigator 
managed to land there, but eventually died on the 
island after their distress calls went unanswered. 
Amelia Earhart’s lifelong dedication to prove that 
women can excel in their chosen professions is a 
great inspiration. Amelia was aware of the hazards 
in her mission, but she chose to face them head-on. 
As she put it, “Never interrupt someone doing what 
you said couldn’t be done.”

lessons.fullText:
It’s the Best Time  
to Be Alive 
The news is chock-full of disasters – 
shootings, terrorism, rape – and it seems like 
every time you tune in, things are getting 
worse. The constant stream of bad news 
often makes it seem like the future is bleak – 
or even that the self-destruction of society is 
imminent. 
But is this really the case? 
The media fixates on the most horrifying 
news because people eat it up. Of course, this 
results in big paydays for the networks and 
advertisers. But when we step back and 
consider the broader historical context, the 
truth is that today is the best time to be alive.  
If you’re not convinced, read on… 
We Live Longer 
Nowadays, the average life expectancy 
worldwide is just over 70 years. That's more 
than double what it was a hundred years ago. 
In those days, people were lucky to make it to 
their early 30s. Most of us would already be 
past our prime! 
Part of the reason for the boost in life 
expectancy is a drastic reduction in infant 
mortality rates. In the early 1900s, 1 in 5 
babies would die before their first birthday. 
These days, it's only 1 in 25. Still not perfect, 
but keep in mind that's the average for the 
entire world, which includes even the poorest 
and most war-torn areas.

who doesn’t want to

Vocabulary 


 
 
There’s Less Poverty 
Since 1990, the percentage of people around the 
world who live in extreme poverty has dropped 
by over 25%. If you go all the way back to 1900, 
the decrease approaches a whopping 60%.  
Per capita income has grown fivefold in the past 
century – from $2,000 to $10,000. Although 
there is still work to be done, we have made 
substantial progress towards eliminating 
extreme poverty. 
Improvements in Education 
Knowing how to read and write is something we 
might take for granted nowadays – but a 
century ago, more than half of the Earth's 
population was illiterate. These days, literacy 
levels are at a historic high of 84% and 
climbing. 
Education is now more accessible than ever, 
especially as the internet puts unlimited 
amounts of information at our fingertips. The 
ability to learn online is very empowering, and 
if governments prioritize connectivity for all 
their citizens, it will go a long way towards 
leveling the playing field economically. 
In addition, the internet helps us interact with 
people from different cultures and viewpoints, 
so we can gain a global perspective instead of 
remaining secluded in our local communities. 
Violence is Decreasing 
No, we haven’t reached the pinnacle of world 
peace just yet. But we’re the closest we’ve been 
in the past 50 years.

Vocabulary 


 
 
Although the headlines and social media might 
give the impression that the world is a powder 
keg… the statistics don’t lie. The number of 
wars (including civil wars and other armed 
conflicts) is going down, and the number of 
casualties is at its lowest point in decades. 
In addition, the homicide rate has been 
declining worldwide, and violence against 
women and children - including physical and 
sexual abuse, has also fallen since 1990. 
Although the reduction is unevenly distributed 
across geographic regions, there are grounds 
for optimism.  
Doomsday Is Not Upon Us 
On average, the world is much safer and more 
prosperous than it was even one or two 
generations ago. So why this sense of 
impending doom? 
One reason is that, thanks to the world’s 
interconnectedness, we are far more cognizant 
of disasters nowadays – regardless of where 
they are happening. Another factor is that the 
human brain is hard-wired by evolution to 
retain information about danger instinctually. 
But when we look at the facts, we realize that 
life is better than it's ever been.  
There is just one worrisome metric, and it has 
to do with the environment. Carbon dioxide 
levels in the atmosphere and global 
temperature have been creeping steadily 
upwards over the past century. This could 
cause major disruption to the global climate 
unless we reduce our carbon output and 
transition to clean energy.

lessons.fullText:
Five of History’s Biggest  
Business Blunders 
No one is immune from stupidity – not even 
the leadership of big companies. Sometimes 
terrible decisions are made, and after the dust 
settles the rest of the world asks, “What on 
earth were they thinking?” Read on to learn 
about companies that blew it in the business 
world. 
 
Excite Says ‘No’ to Buying Google 
 
Google has become such a staple of our 
internet experience that it is now a word in the 
dictionary. But back when Google was just a 
fledgling company in Silicon Valley, it was 
available for sale. Excite.com (now known as 
Ask.com) had the opportunity to buy Google 
for the bargain price of $750,000 – and they 
turned it down. Today, Google is worth nearly 
$365 billion, and the leaders of Excite.com are 
probably still kicking themselves to this day. 
 
Kodak Falls Behind the Times 
 
At one point, Kodak was a giant in the film 
industry – but now it is just a small-time 
player. Once a pioneer in technology, Kodak 
completely failed to capitalize on the surge of 
digital photography.  
 
When the inventor of the digital camera 
showed his invention to Kodak management,

Blockbuster Could Have Owned Netflix 
 
Another tale of a business decision that 
spelled doom for a company is that of 
Blockbuster, which once had nearly 8,000 
video-rental stores in the U.S. In the early 
2000s, a company called Netflix – which was 
providing DVD rentals by mail – approached

At the time, Netflix was in the red and 
Blockbuster decided to pass on the purchase. 
When Netflix later launched on-demand 
streaming over the internet, Blockbuster 
scrambled to play catch-up – but it was too 
late. Blockbuster went under in 2013, and 
Netflix is now worth nearly $20 billion.

$3,900 business class flight for just $39 – and

Who doesn’t love a bargain? 
 
Sometimes an attempt to innovate is actually

Conspiracy Theories  
That Were True 
A conspiracy theory is a claim that groups of 
people or organizations have joined forces to 
cause or cover up illegal or harmful actions. 
Conspiracy theories often seem outlandish, 
and their proponents appear to be paranoid. 
But maybe we shouldn't dismiss these 
claims out of hand – here are three 
conspiracy theories that turned out to be true. 
Government-mandated alcohol 
poisoning in the U.S. 
Alcoholic beverages were banned in the U.S. 
from 1920 to 1933, and there was a booming 
black market for alcohol produced in 
clandestine operations. Traditional efforts to 
crack down on alcohol consumption weren’t 
working, so the government adopted a more 
nefarious strategy.  
It ordered manufacturers of industrial alcohol 
to add deadly chemicals such as mercury, zinc, 
and even gasoline, in the hopes that a dose of 
poison would dissuade people from seeking 
an alcohol-fueled buzz. This led to the deaths 
of approximately 10,000 people as well as 
countless serious illnesses.

together 
outlandish = strange, crazy 
dismiss out of hand = 
dismiss immediately, 
without giving it any 
thought 
booming = large, growing, 
and very active 
black market = illegal 
buying and selling 
crack down on = apply 
strong disciplinary action 
to, in order to reduce 
nefarious = evil 
dissuade = persuade 
someone NOT to do 
something 
buzz = pleasant feeling of 
being slightly intoxicated 
Vocabulary 


 
 
The Nayirah Testimony 
Nayirah was a 15-year old girl from Kuwait 
whose testimony about the atrocities in the 
country helped justify the Gulf War in 1991. 
She gave a sobbing statement that she had 
witnessed Iraqi soldiers invading hospitals, 
removing babies from incubators and leaving 
them to die. Nayirah’s words were widely 
publicized and moved many Americans to 
support the war – but some believed her story 
was fabricated.  
Afterwards, it was revealed that Nayirah was 
actually the daughter of the Kuwaiti 
ambassador to the U.S., and her testimony had 
been arranged by a PR firm. They had 
conducted research to find the best way to 
sway public opinion in support of the war, 
and concocted the incubator story as part of 
the strategy.  
The CIA’s Mind Control 
Experiments 
The CIA program MKUltra ran from 1953-
1964, ostensibly to develop biological and 
chemical weapons for use in the Cold War. But 
it ballooned into an effort to discover 
substances that could brainwash people, 
induce amnesia, and otherwise alter one’s 
mental and physical state.  
testimony = statement in a 
case of justice 
sobbing = crying loudly and 
uncontrollably 
witnessed = seen 
invading = entering by 
force, without permission 
incubators = machines that 
can keep a premature baby 
warm and alive until it 
develops more

imagined, made up from 
nothing

relations company 
concocted = cleverly

expanded

emotions 
amnesia = loss of memory 
Vocabulary 


 
 
The CIA established partnerships with 
hospitals, prisons, and universities in order to 
do their experiments, many of which were not 
consensual – covert drug tests were 
performed on "unwitting subjects."  
The extent of the damage caused will never 
fully be known, since most of the project's 
records were destroyed by order of the CIA 
director in 1973. Only a small cache of 
documents, which had been miscategorized as 
financial records, survived the purge. 
The conspiracies continue… 
People used to ridicule the lunatics who 
claimed the government was spying on us – 
but as recently as 2013, the cover was blown 
on the National Security Agency's illegal 
surveillance program. The NSA has been 
eavesdropping on American citizens for 
years in the name of national security. 
It appears that no government, past or 
present, is immune to manipulating people 
and situations for its own purposes. The 
claims of conspiracy theories might not be so 
crazy after all – so now it’s up to us to learn 
to separate fact from fiction.

lessons.title: Cultural Perceptions of Time
lessons.fullText:
Cultural Perceptions of Time 
Time may be a universal and inflexible law of 
physics, but the way it shapes our everyday lives is 
largely dependent on cultural conditioning.   
Since the industrial revolution at the end of the 
nineteenth century, much of the Western world has 
treated time much as it would a commodity; 
Western cultures organize much of everyday life 
around schedules, appointments and deadlines 
and place great emphasis on the value of not 
‘wasting time.’  
This is quite different from how time has 
traditionally been viewed in many cultures in 
Africa, the Middle East, Latin America and 
Southeast Asia, where relationships, community 
routines and seasonal patterns have a prominent 
role to play in the pace of everyday life.   
A lack of awareness about these nuances in cultural 
perceptions of time can cause serious problems 
when it comes to cross-cultural communication and 
coordination in diplomacy and business.   
The field of study known as ‘chronemics’ addresses 
the ways in which perceptions of time influence 
behavior and interactions, as well as the cultural 
roots of such perceptions.

modified 
conditioning = 
behavioural training

product or service 
that can be used to 
gain profit

date before which 
something must be 
completed

periods of the year

international relations 
between countries

 According to the discipline, time perceptions 
can broadly be divided into monochronic and 
polychronic perspectives.  The former 
conceives of time in terms of fixed units that 
structure everyday life, while the latter has a 
more fluid conception which does not 
demand strict adherence to timetables.   
Much of the Western world could be 
considered monochronic, while many of the 
countries in Africa, the Middle East, Latin 
America and Southeast Asia abide by a 
polychronic conception of time (with the 
exception of Japan, Taiwan and South Korea in 
Asia).      
Another way of imagining the difference is in 
terms of the extent to which a culture is ruled 
by time and the corresponding pace at which 
everyday life is lived.  At one end of the 
spectrum is the United States, where there is 
a 
marked 
emphasis 
on 
organization, 
efficiency, and punctuality.  It is likely that the 
importance placed on time management in the 
U.S. is directly linked to the materialistic 
orientation of its mainstream culture, and 
has its roots in the pursuit of the ‘American 
Dream.’   
At the other extreme, there are cultures for 
which time has virtually no meaning, such as

Vocabulary 


 
 
the indigenous Pirahã tribe of Brazil, whose 
language has been the source of intense debate 
among linguists due to its perplexing 
grammatical and syntax structure.  Of 
particular interest is the nature of its verb 
tenses (or lack thereof). The language itself 
seems to preclude anything resembling a 
Western monochronic conception of time.   
The aforementioned examples illustrate the 
degree of divergence in how time is 
perceived across world cultures, and of course 
there are many conceptions of time and 
lifestyles that fall between these two extremes 
– and both concepts have their pros and cons.   
The monochronic view with its fast-paced, 
goal-oriented efficiency leads to heightened 
levels of production, yet this may come at the 
expense of relationships and sanity.  The 
merits of the polychronic perspective include 
stronger interpersonal ties and a more relaxed 
lifestyle, but the trade-off is that progress may 
be sluggish.  
In today’s globalized world, it remains to be 
seen whether one of these perspectives will 
prevail over the other or whether they will 
converge at some point in the future.

lessons.title: Cyberbullying on the Rise
lessons.fullText:
Cyberbullying on the Rise 
If you open a newspaper or do a Google search, 
you’ll find a wealth of current articles about 
cyberbullying and its consequences. Although 
some try to excuse it as normal teenage antics, 
cyberbullying can cause psychological trauma 
and even lead to suicide. It is indisputably on 
the rise, and one reason is because it’s so easy. 
A few words on a keyboard, then a post to a 
social media site, and the torment begins… 
and escalates. 
The Evolution of Bullying 
In the past, bullying actually used to take a bit 
of work. A bully would corner his or her victim 
in the schoolyard, administer a beating either 
alone or with the help of a few like-minded 
friends. Or the bully would start a rumor, 
nurture it, and wait for it to spread. Bullying 
took more effort, and time. 
That’s not the case any longer. Now, videos go 
viral in no time. In cyberspace, anyone can 
make hateful or humiliating posts and have 
them seen by countless people in the blink of 
an eye. 
a wealth of = a lot of 
indisputably = definitely; it 
cannot be disputed 
torment = torture, causing 
mental or physical pain 
escalates = gets worse, more 
intense 
corner = trap someone in a 
corner or a confined place 
where they cannot escape 
like-minded = people who 
think similarly 
nurture = help or encourage 
it to develop 
go viral = spread extremely 
fast over the internet 
humiliating = extremely 
embarrassing; makes 
someone feel intense shame 
 
Vocabulary 
b l


 
 
Types of Cyberbullying 
Cyberbullying typically involves slander, 
harassment, and sometimes stalking. It’s 
obviously not physical – no one can punch you 
online. It does, however, often derive from, or 
lead to, physical bullying; and you might be 
surprised at how inventive cyberbullies can be 
when it comes to causing harm. 
In his article on Cyberbullying Tactics 2015, 
Michael Nuccitelli, Psy.D., identifies 42 different 
types of cyberbullying. It’s not possible to talk 
about all of them within the scope of this article, 
but here are a few examples. 
1. Blogobullying 
Can you imagine someone creating and 
devoting a blog to the specific purpose of 
targeting one child? It happens, and it’s 
one of the most vicious forms of 
cyberbullying. Cyberbullies know how to 
draw traffic to defamatory blogs. And of 
course we know that the Internet is forever 
– this type of bullying can dog a child for 
years, and could even hurt him or her 
when applying for jobs or college 
admission. 
2. Cyber Harassment 
slander = false and 
malicious statements 
about someone 
harassment = purposefully 
irritating or attacking 
someone, often 
persistently 
stalking = constantly 
following a person when 
the attention is 
unwelcome or threatening 
punch = hit with a fist (a 
tightly closed hand) 
derive from = originate in 
inventive = creative in 
inventing new things 
scope = range or extent of 
information or activity 
targeting = focusing 
specifically on 
vicious = cruel 
draw = attract 
dog = when something 
bad continues to follow 
and accompany someone 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
This goes beyond the occasional rude or 
crude comments. It’s a constant, persistent 
barrage, sometimes involving hundreds, 
or even thousands, of messages in a single 
day. To the person being harassed, it is like 
being confined in a room and subjected to 
24/7 abuse. 
3. Digital Piracy Inclusion 
With this form of attack, the victim is 
encouraged to pirate copyrighted content. 
The cyberbully then reports the victim to 
the authorities. This can be very 
damaging in terms of legal ramifications. 
4. Social Exclusion 
Children all want to be included in a peer 
group, and being left out can be agonizing. 
With social exclusion, the bully encourages 
others to “unfriend” the victim on social 
media sites. It’s a very old tactic, with a 
modern twist. 
5. Impersonation 
This is a kind of identity theft. Sometimes 
called “imping,” it involves impersonating 
the victim and making offensive comments 
under his/her name on social media sites. 
crude = vulgar, offensive, 
disgusting or sexually 
explicit 
barrage = an 
overwhelming and 
continuous delivery of 
words or attacks 
confined = trapped with 
no way to escape 
24/7 = constant, all day 
long, all week long 
pirate = download or copy 
illegally, without paying 
for it 
the authorities = the 
police or the officials in 
charge of administering 
the law

consequences

age and social status 
agonizing = extremely 
painful 
a modern twist = a 
modern change 
impersonating = 
pretending to be another 
person 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
This can lead to the person being 
ostracized not just online, but in person. 
Often, the target is unaware of what has 
happened until the damage is already 
done. 
How can Cyberbullying be Stopped? 
It is not enough to tell kids and teens to simply 
“get over it” or develop a thicker skin – 
cyberbullying goes beyond innocent teasing. 
Nowadays, laws are being made to deal 
specifically with the problem of cyberbullying – 
but legislation is far from a surefire solution to 
the problem.  
Instead, it is imperative for parents and teachers 
to be proactive and try to nip cyberbullying in 
the bud. Pay attention to what your child is doing 
and experiencing online, and educate him or her 
on the virtues of the golden rule. 
 
Sources & Further Reading:

• Advice for Parents 
• Current Cyberbullying Laws

lessons.title: Development of Artificial Intelligence
lessons.fullText:
Artificial Intelligence 
Over the past sixty years, the field of artificial intelligence (AI) has developed from 
being nothing more than an elaborate concept 
to having a central role in an increasingly 
diverse array of areas of individual, social and 
economic life.  In its broadest sense, AI involves 
endowing machines and computers with an 
intellectual capacity to calculate and make 
informed decisions.   
In spite of periodic lulls in funding and 
technological advancement over the course of 
its existence as a field of research, AI has now 
reached a state of advancement that has 
exceeded many of its early proponents’ own 
expectations.  Robots today are becoming 
responsible for an ever-greater number of 
human 
tasks, 
which 
they 
carry 
out 
autonomously and often more efficiently than 
their human counterparts. 
The idea of replicating the workings of the 
human mind in an artificially-created being 
existed long before mankind acquired the 
technological tools necessary to implement it.  
It originates in a philosophical conception of 
the mind as a system of rules which govern 
thought and behavior.   
However, AI as a concrete field of study was 
born in the summer of 1956 at a conference in 
Dartmouth.  A group of interested researchers 
gathered around the premise that every aspect 
of intellectual activity could theoretically be 
described in such precise detail as to make it 
possible to program machines and computers 
to replicate these activities.  With a scientific

complex 
array = a large range or  
number 
lulls = low points in 
activity

support or are in favor of 
something 
autonomously = 
independently, without 
help

influence, manage 
concrete = definite, 
clearly-defined 
premise = an idea from 
which a logical argument 
is developed

Over the next twenty years, researchers and

A shortfall in funding in the mid-1970’s briefly 
cast the future of the field into doubt, until the 
commercial potential of AI was discovered 
through the development of expert systems, 
which simulated human knowledge and 
expertise in a given specialist field.  The Digital 
Equipment Corporation saved an estimated 
$40 million a year thanks to its purchase of an 
expert system, which was the first to be used 
for commercial purposes.   
With the lucrative potential of AI thus proven, 
the area continued to expand and attract 
investment into the 1990’s and early 21st 
century, achieving unprecedented levels of 
success. 
The state of AI today can be characterized by a 
seemingly exponential proliferation of areas 
that have come under the responsibility of 
intelligent machines.  In the realm of everyday 
life, the personal assistant feature of most new 
smartphones can do anything from managing 
our busy schedules by altering appointment 
details and informing other parties that you 
are running late, to monitoring our health and

fitness regimes and making suggestions for

Meanwhile 
in 
the 
economic 
sphere, 
automation is fast becoming the general rule; at 
present there are 1.1 million working robots in 
the world, and in the automobile industry 80% 
of the car assembly is now completed by 
robots.  It is no wonder that private 
investment in the AI sector has been expanding 
at an average rate of 62 percent a year for the 
past four years.   
These trends indicate that AI’s trajectory is one 
of future expansion and advancement.  There is 
much 
speculation 
among 
scholars 
and 
industry experts about what this implies for 
the human race.   
On the optimistic side, people see potential in 
AI to make life far easier and more enjoyable by 
catering to an ever greater number of human 
needs.     
On the negative side, some assert that humans 
will gradually be displaced by machines in 
every aspect of the job market.  Given the 
astonishing pace at which AI is currently 
developing, neither of these scenarios seems 
implausible at present.   
How things unfold in the future is largely a 
matter of collective human choice about the 
role we would like to see AI play in our lives, 
and of whether we are capable of putting this 
choice into practice.

lessons.title: Drowning in Debt
lessons.fullText:
Drowning in Debt 
Several years after the recent recession, many 
Americans have a shared handicap: massive 
debt. Between school loans, credit card debt, and 
mortgages, countless individuals carry financial 
burdens which seem impossible to escape.  
It’s tempting to point fingers. Was it the fault of 
the lenders who issued mortgages to individuals 
who would be likely to default? The people who 
chose to borrow more than they could repay? 
Was it the colleges that charged exorbitant 
amounts for tuition… or the unreasonably high 
interest rates?  
The debt crisis is likely a result of a combination 
of these factors. But perhaps identifying the 
culprit is irrelevant – or at least, a secondary 
concern. The bigger, more urgent question is: 
How can indebted Americans improve their 
situation? 
The number of students who graduate college 
not just with their diploma, but also with a 
sizeable amount of money to pay back, increases 
at an alarming rate each year. The class of 2014 
carries more student debt than any class 
preceding it.  
A record 70% of undergraduate students in that 
class required the assistance of loans, with the 
average student owing a total of $33,000 – and 
that’s just for a bachelor’s degree. There are 
also 15% of graduate students who leave school 
with a six-figure tab.

mortgages = loans taken 
out to buy a house

someone for a bad thing 
that happened 
default = declare yourself 
unable to pay back a 
mortgage

expensive than customary

college

of money you have to pay 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Does this mean that students should not pursue 
college degrees? It’s not that simple. Having a 
college education still results in higher lifetime 
earnings. According to the experts, one rule of 
thumb is to avoid accepting loans that would be 
higher than your future entry-level salary. For 
instance, if you’re likely to earn $25,000 in the 
first year of your intended career as a social 
worker, do not take on more than that amount in 
student debt.  
It’s also important for students to consider a 
variety of options. Rather than blindly signing 
on for a liberal arts education or specializing in 
an obscure subject, consider less pricey options 
like state schools or community colleges – and 
think about the marketplace demand for people 
with your degree.  
Student loans aren’t the only problem. In 
addition to educational debt, there is also credit 
card debt – the average American household 
owes over $7,000 – and mortgages, for which 
the average American household owes over 
$155,000.  
With debt payments encroaching on the family 
budget, Americans are less likely to spend on 
discretionary purchases, which then hinders 
economic growth. Despite these eye-popping 
figures for overall household debt, this number 
is actually down from 2010, indicating a move in 
the right direction. 
If you’re deep in debt, here are a few 
recommendations. The first step is to add up all 
your financial obligations so you can understand

or analyzing

exactly what you are dealing with. Then make a

You may need to adopt a frugal lifestyle and cut

Finally, whenever possible, submit more than

in interest and accelerate your progress towards 
becoming debt free.

lessons.title: Finland's Approach to Education
lessons.fullText:
Finland’s Approach to Education 
Finland is highly regarded across the globe for its consistently excellent results in 
the Program for International Student Assessment 
(PISA). Not only do Finnish students excel at subjects 
like reading, science and mathematics, their high 
school graduation rate is at an astonishing 93%, with 
an average of 2 out of 3 students going on to college.  
How are Finnish schools different from a global 
perspective? 
The emphasis is on learning, not 
competition. 
The lack of standardization in Finnish schools means 
that there are no scored tests, only one mandatory 
exam for students at 17 years old. All tests before this 
exam are not graded or compared, but are instead 
used as feedback on the learning progress of each 
student.  
This allows students’ education to be tailored to their 
own strengths and weaknesses. Instead of ‘ticking the 
box’ on a test which is then filed away, the 
evaluations indicate how well the student is learning, 
and the areas in which he or she needs help. 
highly regarded = 
others have a good 
opinion about 
 
standardization = 
making everything the 
same 
 
mandatory = 
obligatory; you must 
do it; not optional 
 
filed away = put away 
into an archive 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Finnish teachers are highly educated 
and innovative. 
In Finland, teaching is a prestigious career. Teachers 
are respected and appreciated at the same level as 
doctors or lawyers. They are highly qualified, with all 
teachers required to hold a Master’s Degree. There is 
only one academic program for those who aspire to 
be teachers, and this education is fully subsidized by 
the state. Even after the rigorous program, the 
selection process is so tough that only the top 10 
percent of graduates are then accepted into teaching 
careers.  
Schools have creative autonomy to 
ensure maximum learning efficiency. 
The Finns understand that each school may require a 
different approach depending on the needs of the 
attending students, so they allow each school to do 
what serves its students best. Teachers follow state 
curriculum guidelines that tell them what to teach, 
but each teacher has the freedom to decide how to 
teach.  
The curriculum is filled with plenty of art, music and 
science. Different methods of teaching are embraced 
and utilized, which leads to greater creativity.  
innovative = creative, 
inventing new ideas 
and methods 
aspire = strongly 
desire; have an 
ambition to do 
something 
fully subsidized = 
completely paid for 
rigorous = following 
strict standards, 
thorough and 
complete, intense 
autonomy = 
independence; can act 
as they want 
approach = method, 
way of doing things 
guidelines = rules or 
suggestions 
curriculum = the 
collection of courses 
embraced = welcomed, 
supported, adopted 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Students are given room to grow and 
develop healthily. 
Finnish people recognize the need for kids to be kids. 
School is not mandatory until the age of 7, with 
homework rarely assigned until their teens. Longer 
recesses give students time to develop socially and 
physically by playing outside, enabling their minds to 
decompress and freshen up for the next lesson.  
Students receive individual attention to 
help them keep up. 
In a somewhat unorthodox approach to other 
Western countries, a ‘no child is left behind’ approach 
means that all classes contain pupils at different 
levels of learning ability. The low student to teacher 
ratio (approximately 1 teacher for every 15 students) 
enables teachers to know each student exceptionally 
well, so that no student falls through the cracks.  
There are no special remedial classes – instead, 
children who are struggling receive extra support

Education is viewed as preparing kids for life, so

Common Health & Exercise  
Myths Debunked 
There is a lot of misinformation out there about 
health and exercise. Someone at the gym says 
something, and then that “fact” gets passed around 
through friends and acquaintances until it ends up 
online.  
 
Many people would like to eat better or get in 
shape, but end up getting bad advice that doesn't 
work – and then they become discouraged and give 
up. Let’s put an end to a few common myths about 
health and exercise right here and now. 
 
Myth #1 – “Treadmills are easier on your 
knees than asphalt” 
 
One of the biggest reasons people don't run is that 
they're afraid it will damage their knees. While it's 
true that over-stressing your knees by running too 
much is bad for you, using a treadmill, as opposed 
to running outside, doesn't actually change 
anything. When you run, your body weight comes 
down on your knee at an accelerated pace. So 
whether you're coming down on asphalt or rubber 
doesn't make much difference.

or incorrect information

who you know casually, 
but who are not close 
enough to be 
considered friends

physically fit and strong

informal phrase 
meaning to end or stop 
something intentionally 
(we usually “put an end 
to” bad things)

backwards-moving belt 
so you can run on it and 
stay in one place 
asphalt = the hard black 
material that roads are 
made of 
as opposed to = in 
contrast to; instead of 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
What can protect your knees is mixing up running 
with other cardio workouts; such as using an 
elliptical machine or a bicycle. 
 
Myth #2 –  
“Swimming is great for weight loss” 
 
Swimming is good for a lot of things, mainly 
increasing lung capacity and toning muscles. It is 
not, however, the best formula for weight loss. The 
buoyancy of the human body means that 
exercising in water doesn't work the body as much 
as exercising outside of water. For the same reason, 
a lot of fitness classes for elderly people are done 
in swimming pools.  
 
That isn't to say that swimming is a bad workout, it 
just needs to be done alongside other more fat-
burning exercises like cardio and strength 
training when trying to lose weight. 
 
Myth #3 – “Fatty foods make you fat” 
 
This one seems very logical – after all, “you are 
what you eat,” right? However, the science behind it 
doesn't quite work that way. The truth is that fat is 
a necessary part of your diet. Excess body fat is the

joints

Vocabulary 


 
 
result of the energy imbalance that occurs when 
more calories are consumed than are used – 
regardless of the source of those calories. Although 
overindulging in fatty foods will result in weight 
gain, a more common cause of obesity is actually 
eating excess carbohydrates such as sugar. 
 
Myth #4 – “Sugar is healthier than High 
Fructose Corn Syrup” 
 
High fructose corn syrup or HFCS is often vilified 
as one of the causes of poor health in the United 
States, and natural sugar is often identified as a 
“healthier” alternative.  
 
Unfortunately this is not true. Sugar and HFCS both 
cause a spike in blood sugar levels which, when 
consumed regularly, leads to obesity and Type 2 
diabetes. The true risk factor is not HFCS 
specifically, but one’s total intake of sugars of any 
kind. 
 
Now if you hear someone passing along one of 
these health myths, you can politely quash that 
rumor with the facts.

lessons.title: Helicopter Parents
lessons.fullText:
Helicopter Parents 
The term “helicopter parent” refers to an overly 
vigilant parent who seems to hover constantly 
over his or her child. Although helicopter parents 
may think they are helping and protecting their 
kids, they may actually be contributing to 
developmental problems.  
A helicopter parent is always concerned – some 
might say obsessed – about possible harm to 
their child. A helicopter parent is always there to 
protect the child from threats both real and 
imagined.  
They also try to ensure that their child 
experiences no stress, and get the child out of 
whatever scrape they’re in – even if it’s the 
child’s own fault!  
Every parent feels a natural and appropriate 
concern for their child’s well-being – but 
helicopter parents cross the line into over-
protectiveness.  
Such behavior can stunt the child’s emotional 
development and impair his or her ability to 
make sensible decisions in adulthood.

careful, watches too much 
hover = stay in the air 
above the target 
obsessed = thinking too 
much about something, to 
an unhealthy degree 
scrape = trouble (usually 
minor trouble) 
cross the line = pass the 
limit of what is 
appropriate 
over-protectiveness = 
protecting too much 
stunt = prevent from 
growing 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
What are some of the possible repercussions of 
helicopter parenting? 
1. Your child will never learn how to be 
accountable for his own behavior 
You’re always there when he needs you, 
always bailing him out. When he gets in 
trouble at school, you march to the principal’s 
office and convince him to let your child off 
the hook. Then you don’t deal with the issue 
at home. By doing this, you’re teaching your 
child that there are no consequences for 
misbehavior; that he never has to admit that 
he’s done something wrong or try to make it 
right. He’s going to carry that sense of 
entitlement through to adulthood, and you 
can bet that employers aren’t going to be 
nearly as lenient as you are. 
2. Your child will never learn how to handle 
struggle and failure 
You do her homework whenever it becomes 
the least bit difficult, never letting her take on 
a challenge or struggle to solve a tough 
problem. If you keep this up, she’ll never 
learn how to take risks or persevere. Also, 
repercussions = 
consequences / results 
(usually negative ones)

for your actions 
bailing him out = getting 
him out of trouble 
let your child off the hook 
= not punish the child for 
something bad he/she did

behavior

you are special and

Vocabulary 


 
 
you’re reinforcing the concept that failure is 
never an option – leaving her unprepared to 
face the challenges of adult life outside your 
protective bubble. 
3. Your child will have fragile self-esteem 
Perhaps you lavish words of praise on your 
child, telling him daily how special he is and 
how he can do anything at all that he sets his 
mind to. And yet you constantly interfere in 
everything he tries to do, with the goal of 
ensuring the best possible outcome. This sets 
the precedent that your child can’t do 
anything without your help. When your child 
grows up, he may experience a paradoxical 
feeling of seeing himself as special and 
entitled, yet being crushed by the slightest 
failure. 
4. It will be difficult for your child to have a 
healthy relationship 
If you raise a spoiled child who thinks that he 
doesn’t need to pick up after himself or learn 
basic life skills – then good luck to him in 
finding a life partner. Most rational adults 
want an equal – they don’t want to babysit. 
You need to let your child spread his wings, fly 
on his own, and even fall back to earth on

Vocabulary 


 
 
occasion. If you don’t, he may end up in a

scenario, continue to “take care of him” the 
way you did. Worst case scenario, he’ll end 
up with someone who controls and 
manipulates him, and he’ll be helpless to stand 
on his own two feet. 
If you’re disposed to hovering, it can be hard to 
stop. But if you allow your kids to handle 
challenges without your help, they’ll become self-
confident and independent. When they fail, let 
them learn how to bounce back. And when your 
kids misbehave, let them suffer the consequences. 
They’ll end up thanking you for it.

lessons.title: History's Heroic Dogs
lessons.fullText:
History’s Heroic Dogs 
There’s a reason why dogs are considered “man’s 
best friend.” Every owner has had a dog that he knew 
would save his life if tragedy struck. Throughout 
history, there are countless amazing stories of dogs 
saving their owners from intruders, disasters, and 
wild animals.  
Although maybe not the ideal replacement for a 
bodyguard or a good life insurance policy, a good 
dog will do everything it can to keep you and your 
family safe.  Here are a few stories of heroic dogs 
whose deeds have gone down in history. 
Saint Guinefort 
There is one heroic dog that is actually considered a 
saint by the local community. According to legend, 
Guinefort was a greyhound owned by a French 
knight in the 1200s. One day, the knight left his 
young child alone with Guinefort for the day. When 
he returned he couldn’t find his child, but saw 
Guinefort with blood across its face.  
Fearing that his dog had just slaughtered and 
possibly eaten his young boy, the knight killed 
Guinefort in a rage. Moments later, the knight found 
his child as well as the dead snake that Guinefort had 
killed in order to protect the boy.

buried Guinefort and built a shrine to the dog, which

The St. Bernard is now associated with hundreds of 
stories of saving people’s lives, especially children, 
and that’s mostly because of Barry, the heroic St. 
Bernard from Switzerland. Barry lived near a 
monastery in Switzerland from 1800-1812. Over 
that time, he is credited with rescuing at least 40 
people who had gotten lost or trapped in the snow.

a mountain to rescue a small child when the snow

Barry, and Barry carried him all the way down the 
mountain. Barry is such a beloved piece of Swiss 
history that after his death he was stuffed, and he 
now has a place in the Swiss Natural History 
Museum.

heroic deeds. In the winter of 1925, the town of

Interesting Recent Inventions 
 
Think our modern world already has everything 
you could possibly imagine? Think again. 
Human creativity knows no bounds, and new 
products and technologies are being invented all 
the time. Here are a few of the notable things 
invented recently. 
 
The Hoverboard 
 
Who hasn’t dreamed of being Marty McFly from 
Back To The Future II, zipping around Biff on his 
flying skateboard? Given that the 1989 film 
imagined the “future” in the year 2015 (our 
present and soon to be past), this product was 
developed in the nick of time.  
 
However, the technology is not quite up to par 
compared to the thrilling device in the science 
fiction movie. There are limitations – for 
instance, the board will only levitate over 
conductive materials like copper and 
aluminum, flies just an inch off the ground, and 
can only operate for fifteen minutes at a time.  
 
Also, only ten prototypes are on the market, 
all at the whopping sum of $10,000—meaning 
only someone like Michael J. Fox himself can 
afford it. 
 
But when you consider the fact that computers 
used to take up entire rooms, and now they fit 
into our pockets – the possibility of a more

limit 
 
zipping = moving very fast 
and effortlessly 
 
in the nick of time = exactly 
at the right time before a 
deadline 
 
thrilling = very exciting 
 
conductive materials =

electricity

of the product

for sale

(informal) 
 
take up = occupy space 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
versatile hoverboard in the future doesn’t 
seem so far-fetched. Perhaps it’s only a 
matter of time before the technology is 
refined and the hoverboard becomes a 
household item.  
 
Wireless Electricity 
 
We are already doing away with so many 
cords: telephone cords, Internet cords—
why not eliminate the need for cords 
altogether?  
 
WiTricity, a Massachusetts company, wants 
to do just that – without the use of batteries. 
They have developed a plug-in coil that 
produces a magnetic field, which can power 
all electronic devices up to several meters 
away – even through walls. So far, this 
technology has been applied to Toyota 
electric cars and Intel PCs, but WiTricity is 
looking at the big picture. So say goodbye 
to the days of tripping over your power 
cords. We’ll soon be operating completely 
wirelessly.  
 
3-D Printing 
 
3-D printing has exploded over the past 
few years, and it is bound to revolutionize 
nearly all types of production. These 
printers are able to apply successive layers 
of glass, metal, plastic, and other materials 
in order to build objects designed on a 
digital blueprint.

imagine 
 
it’s only a matter of time = it 
will definitely happen at some 
point in the future 
 
refined = made better and more 
perfect by improving small 
details 
 
doing away with = removing; 
not using anymore

that are gathered together

considering the wider 
perspective on an issue

you fall

(thin covering/level) of material 
after another

of something to be built  
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
This technology is incredibly valuable for a 
number of engineering industries, with the 
potential to streamline manufacturing processes 
and reduce environmental impact.  
 
Some even say we will be able to 3D print edible 
food and even organ replacements in the future. 
Time will tell exactly how 3-D printing will 
transform our lives. 
 
Alert Ring 
 
You know the feeling: your cell phone is buried 
somewhere in your purse, and because you’re 
expecting a call or an email, you periodically feel 
buzzes from within your bag.  
 
After rummaging through all your belongings, 
you finally locate your phone and discover the 
buzz was a figment of your imagination, 
generated by the expectation of a message.  
 
This new invention, a ring whose stone blinks 
when the wearer receives an email, call, or text, 
will end the uncertainty and help you stay on top 
of your messages.  
 
The Selfie Stick 
 
The selfie stick is not exactly a revolutionary idea – 
a photographer in 1925 even used a stick to 
extend the range of his camera. However, the 
modern version of the product hit the market at 
the height of the selfie craze – and has been 
selling like hotcakes.

The Dark Side of  
International Adoption 
Each year, approximately 40,000 children join 
new families via international adoption. The 
procedures and requirements vary from country 
to country – some have well-established systems 
to facilitate the process, while others expressly 
forbid adopting across borders.  
International adoption is often a lengthy and 
costly endeavor, and the amount of paperwork 
may seem onerous. However, it is all done with 
the end goal of providing a loving and stable 
home for the child. 
Adopting a child from another country is usually 
a positive experience for both the family and 
child – but it is not without its problems. 
Trafficking and Abuse  
The demand for healthy, young children from the 
developing world is enormous – especially as 
birth rates in developed countries decline. 
Critics of international adoption believe that this 
demand is fueling nefarious practices in poorer 
countries. With such a large “marketplace,” 
unscrupulous profit-seekers can make a lot of 
money from desperate Western families who

There have even been many cases of children 
being kidnapped from their families and sold to 
orphanages.  
In the aftermath of wars and natural disasters, 
there is often an outpouring of adoption 
requests from foreigners who want to help 
orphaned children. However, special care should 
be taken in these cases. It is possible that some of 
the child’s relatives may have survived but are 
unable to find him/her in the midst of the 
turmoil. 
Due to the problems in the adoption process, 
many countries have tightened their adoption 
regulations considerably. 
Roadblocks to Happiness  
Adopted children may experience a range of 
emotional issues. Recurring feelings of rejection 
and abandonment are quite common. If the 
child’s birth parents are deceased, he or she may 
experience even greater feelings of loss. 
It’s not uncommon for adopted children to feel 
like they don’t fit in, and to have a need to 
understand where they came from. This is part of 
any normal identity formation process, but can

On top of the trauma of being in an unfamiliar 
environment, some adopted children have also 
experienced emotional and physical abuse. The 
combination of these factors can result in the 
child acting out, and many new adoptive parents 
are unprepared to cope with their child’s 
behavioral issues. 
Conclusion  
International adoption has provided many people 
with a nurturing home and opportunities for a 
good life. On the flip side, some adoptees are 
still dealing with the trauma of being stolen from 
their families and sold by human traffickers.  
UNICEF estimates that there are 18 million 
children without parents in the world, and many 
people argue that the exacting regulations are 
restricting these children’s chances of finding a 
loving family. Do the risks of abuse outweigh the 
greater good of international adoptions?

lessons.title: Meditation Ancient and Modern
lessons.fullText:
Meditation – Ancient and Modern 
The practice known as “meditation” encompasses a diverse range of mental and 
physical exercises that have been used across 
cultural and religious contexts throughout history – 
the common characteristic being an effort to focus 
and regulate one’s attention.   
Depending on the context, meditation can be 
practiced in order to connect with the sacred or 
divine, 
to 
focus 
the 
mind 
and 
enhance 
concentration, or to alleviate and prevent a variety 
of mental and physical disorders.   
Historically, meditation has developed within 
religious practice as a means of facilitating the 
worship of deities and sacred objects.  However, it 
has persisted in the Western world, even as 
religious belief declines, due to growing popular 
acceptance of its physical and psychological 
benefits. 
Meditation has its roots deep in human history; 
some scholars claim that it played a key role in 
the final stages of our biological evolution by aiding 
the brain’s development of the capacity for focused 
attention and working memory.

Meditation was a prominent aspect of many 
ancient eastern belief systems, with the first 
known written references dating back to around

which outlined a way to arrive at a more 
profound awareness of the self and one’s 
surroundings 
through 
concentrated 
introspection.   
Similar concerns underlie Taoist concepts as well 
as the Buddhist Zen technique.  Judaism, 
Christianity, and Islam also have traditions of 
disciplined inner reflection undertaken with the 
goal of bringing oneself closer to God.   
In spite of the secular turn that much of the 
Western world has steadily been taking, 
meditation has not lost its appeal. New variants 
of spiritual practices such as the New Age 
movement 
and 
Yoga 
have 
incorporated 
meditation in their routines.  Meanwhile, 
psychologists and counsellors have made use of 
meditation techniques with clients.   
Skeptics may dismiss meditation as a superficial 
fad, but there is an expanding body of scientific 
evidence demonstrating its positive effects. Long-
term meditation appears to result in structural 
changes to the brain – one study showed that 
meditation veterans lose less gray matter as

they age.  Numerous studies have proven that

According to the Mayo Clinic, meditation may 
also help in managing the symptoms of 
illnesses such as heart disease, cancer, anxiety 
and asthma, as well as in contributing to 
emotional well-being by helping to manage 
stress, focus on the present, reduce negative

Despite being a core element of ancient 
religious beliefs and customs, the practice of 
meditation has managed to embed itself 
quite comfortably in the secular West thanks 
to its demonstrated scientific validity.   
For many practitioners, meditation helps 
counterbalance the hectic and disorienting 
nature of modern life.  The practice of 
meditation is remarkable in the degree to 
which it has bridged tradition and modernity 
as well as religion and science.

lessons.title: Motivation
lessons.fullText:
How to Stay 
Motivated 
 
Staying motivated can be a real struggle. 
Sometimes the task at hand is too difficult 
or too tedious to maintain your interest. 
Sometimes you get sidetracked. 
Sometimes you feel crushed by the sheer 
number of your responsibilities, and it 
seems easier to give up or ignore them.  
 
How can we optimize our behavior in 
order to get the job done? Here are a few 
things that can grease the wheels. 
 
Create a Constructive 
Environment 
If your space isn’t conducive to work, 
you’re apt to become scatter-brained. 
Consider the following questions when 
arranging your workspace:  
• Do you have good lighting?  
• Is it noisy?  
• Do your surroundings remind you 
of all the other things that need to 
be accomplished?  
tedious = boring, 
monotonous (no variation 
or interest) 
 
get sidetracked = get 
distracted by something 
that is not in line with your 
main goal 
 
crushed = completely 
destroyed by pressure 
 
sheer = only, without 
considering anything else 
(the number itself is great 
enough to make things 
difficult, regardless of the 
difficulty of the actual 
responsibilities)

something the best it can 
be

things run more smoothly 
 
apt to = have a natural 
tendency to 
 
scatter-brained = 
distracted, thinking about 
many different things 
Vocabulary 


 
 
• Is it too cluttered?  
• Do you have everything needed to 
do your work at hand?  
• Are you inspired or distracted by 
decorations like photos, 
motivational images or quotes, 
plants, etc.?  
Making your workspace a cocoon of 
productivity will help you get down to 
business.  
 
Change Your Routine 
 
Ask yourself: do you feel burnt out? 
Perhaps you’re in a rut, and that’s what is 
slowing you down. If this is the case, try 
changing your habits.  
 
Maybe working at a different time of day, 
or from a different location, will be a 
breath of fresh air. Other things you can 
vary include your meals or background 
music. A change of pace might spark 
some new ideas.

many objects occupying a 
space

to you

space

seriously

routine

differently

your normal routine

Vocabulary 


 
 
Make a List 
 
This is a time-honored trick for 
approaching multiple tasks. A slew of 
chores rattling around in your head 
always seems less daunting and more 
manageable when outlined on paper. And 
the best part of making a list is the 
satisfaction when you can cross off an 
item.  
 
Small Tasks 
 
When writing your to-do list, break large 
jobs down into small, bite-sized parts. For 
instance, if your goal is to write a book, 
don’t consider that a single task. That can 
be intimidating – and you’ll never finish it 
in a day.  
 
Instead, tell yourself, “Today, all I need to 
do is write one dialogue.” Because that 
task is more achievable, you’re more likely 
to dive in and finish.

because it has been useful 
for a long time

around and making lots of 
noise

through some words to 
eliminate them

to be manageable 
 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Set Up a Rewards System 
 
Everybody likes to be compensated for 
their work, and you can reward yourself, 
too. Choose something you enjoy, and then 
set a reasonable goal to reach before you 
can have it. For example, “If I study for an 
hour, then I can relax with one episode of 
my favorite television show.” Setting a 
limit to your leisure makes you less likely 
to binge on it – and you can enjoy your 
reward guilt-free once the work is done. 
 
Take Care of Yourself 
 
Your body is a machine, and in order for it 
to function at its peak, you must keep it 
well oiled. How can you do this? Easy: eat 
healthy food, exercise regularly, sleep 
enough, and don’t push yourself too hard. 
All of these factors improve your physical 
self, which improves your mental acuity 
and helps you feel on top of your game—
and this can supercharge your 
productivity.

your work/effort

b. necessary for survival 
c. something new/different, and pleasant 
 
4. A slew of chores rattling around in your head always seems less

b. clear, obvious to anybody

lessons.title: Oprah Winfrey
lessons.fullText:
Oprah Winfrey 
Oprah Winfrey is a self-made media mogul, 
having succeeded as an entrepreneur, television 
talk show host, actress, publisher, producer, and 
philanthropist. Today, she is one of only seven 
black billionaires in the world. Although Oprah is 
now a household name, she rose to these 
heights from very humble beginnings.  
Winfrey was born to a teenage single mother in a 
small farming community. The name on her birth 
certificate is actually Orpah, but people 
mispronounced it until the misconception stuck. 
Her childhood was marked by hardship, 
including extreme poverty (she often wore potato 
sacks for dresses) and sexual molestation by 
relatives and friends of her mother. After thirteen 
years of such suffering, she fled and moved in 
with her father in Nashville, who prioritized her 
education. 
After winning an oratory contest, she was 
awarded a full ride to Tennessee State 
University, where she studied communication.  
She then rose through the ranks of radio and 
television broadcasting, becoming both the 
youngest news anchor and the first black female 
news anchor of Nashville’s WLAC-TV. In 1978,

success with her own 
efforts

powerful person

who gives to charity or 
good causes

Vocabulary

as well as the local rendition of Dialing for

In 1983, a Chicago TV station recruited Oprah 
to host a low-rated morning talk show called 
AM Chicago. After the charismatic Winfrey 
joined the program, the ratings skyrocketed, 
and the show went from last place to first place. 
It wasn’t long before AM Chicago was renamed 
The Oprah Winfrey Show and expanded to a full 
hour timeslot. Thanks to her mounting 
popularity and fame, Winfrey landed a role in 
Steven Spielberg’s 1985 film The Color Purple, 
which earned her an Academy Award 
nomination for Best Supporting Actress. 
The Oprah Winfrey Show was revolutionary in 
its curiosity, thoughtfulness, generosity of spirit, 
good humor, and empathy. She bucked the 
trend of gossipy talk shows, instead 
concentrating on important issues, with special 
emphasis on confessional therapy in an 
intimate setting. The program was also famous 
for its audience-wide giveaways, and it became 
so wildly popular that it earned $125 million in 
its first year.

Vocabulary 


 
 
Since the takeoff of her talk show, Oprah has 
conquered many other avenues of media, including 
co-founding two television networks, authoring 
five books, publishing two magazines, and 
launching a radio channel.  
Today, Oprah Winfrey is a force to be reckoned 
with. Her powerful influence on public opinion has 
been dubbed “The Oprah Effect,” as her 
endorsements have a profound impact on 
politicians, musicians, charitable organizations, 
and actors. She has also tackled social issues 
including hormone therapy, homosexual rights, 
spirituality, and postpartum depression – some 
even say she has more sway over the American 
people than the president. 
Oprah was also the first black person to rank 
among the 50 most generous Americans, having 
given away over $400 million to educational and 
humanitarian causes. One of her projects is a 
state-of-the-art school for girls in South Africa, 
which is attended by 450 students. 
Despite her dysfunctional upbringing, Oprah 
Winfrey used her talent and determination to 
become an undeniable powerhouse in our 
modern world, and an inspiration to many.

lessons.title: Parenting Around the World
lessons.fullText:
Parenting Styles Around the World 
It’s a given that all parents want what's best for 
their children. But depending on their culture, 
“what’s best” could mean wildly different things.  
Some parents try to keep their kids safe at all 
costs, while others cultivate independence in 
their offspring. There are parents who prioritize 
academic achievement, and other parents who 
just want their children to be healthy and happy, 
regardless of their levels of success. 
It's not just language and food that separate these 
different countries. Let's take a look at how their 
parenting styles differ too.  
Western Europe 
While French parents can seem fairly laid back 
when it comes to parenting, they're actually 
pretty strict. You might not see them fretting 
over every little thing their child does, but respect 
for adults is a non-negotiable. The French also 
take a hands-off approach and expect their kids 
to be independent from an early age.  
Meanwhile, the sociable Spaniards place a huge 
amount of importance on spending time with 
family. Kids who despise early bedtimes would 
love Spain, where parents let their children stay 
up late in order to be with their loved ones.  
British parents take a fairly democratic approach 
to child-rearing. Instead of simply punishing a 
troublesome child in a knee-jerk reaction, they'll 
first explain exactly what they did wrong. They

Norwegian mothers enjoy a generous amount

After a child’s first birthday, he or she spends a 
good portion of the day in daycare. The 
daycare centers are subsidized by the state in 
order to encourage parents to return to the 
workforce.  
In both Norway and Denmark, there is an 
obsession with getting kids as much fresh air 
as possible. Danish parents will park their 
strollers outside the stores while they shop. 
Meanwhile, Norwegian parents often have 
children take their daily nap outside, even if 
it's snowing.  
Africa 
In Kenya and the Democratic Republic of the 
Congo, nobody bats an eye at the idea of 
sharing breastmilk. Most moms carry their

culturally acceptable to nurse anytime and 
anywhere.  
Tight-knit families and communities play a 
major role in caring for children. Occasionally, 
children will go to live with another relative or 
even another family if their own parents are 
overburdened. There is an ethos of shared 
responsibility when it comes to childcare.

China is similar in that grandparents often live 
with the family and participate in a child's

South Koreans are similar in that parents are

Japanese children have a high degree of

United States 
Parents in the United States highly value self-
