lessons.title: Disastrous Dating Pet Peeves
lessons.fullText:
Disastrous Dating 
Pet Peeves 
Dating can be fun and exciting, but the 
foibles of the opposite sex can also drive 
you crazy. Let’s look at the top dating gripes 
from both a male and a female perspective.  
Men on women 
1: Tweeting or Facebooking over dinner is a 
big no-no. If you really want to exasperate 
your date, take a picture of your expensive 
entrée, nibble at it, and then claim you can’t 
possibly eat any more because it’s full of 
calories! 
2: If you are visibly upset about something, 
and we ask what’s wrong, don’t just say 
“nothing” – men prefer candor to guessing 
games. The worst thing you can do is to 
conceal or bottle up your emotions, only to 
unleash them at a later time when the guy 
probably won’t even remember the incident 
you’re still riled up over. 
3: Talking about your ex – regardless of 
whether you’re singing his praises or 
trashing him. This is especially bad on a 
first date – when a girl goes on and on 
about her ex-boyfriend, it’s a major red flag. 
pet peeve = something that 
especially annoys a person 
foibles = minor character flaws 
or strange things about a 
person 
gripes = complaints 
a big no-no = something you 
should definitely not do 
exasperate = make very 
annoyed, impatient, or angry 
entrée = main dish in a 
restaurant 
nibble = eat very tiny bites 
visibly = obviously, it’s easy to 
see 
conceal = hide 
bottle up = keep inside 
unleash = release (especially 
something dangerous) 
riled up = angry and upset 
ex = former romantic partner 
singing his praises = saying 
great things about him 
trashing him = saying terrible 
things about him 
goes on and on = talks without 
stopping 
a red flag = a warning sign that 
danger is ahead 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
4: Overdoing the makeup can also be a 
turnoff. Most men actually prefer a more 
natural look in which makeup is used 
tastefully to accent your best features. 
Don’t plaster on more makeup than 
normal. 
Women on men 
1: Not listening. We all know that men 
sometimes space out, go on autopilot and 
interject with the occasional “yeah” or 
“hmm.” This doesn’t fool women one bit, 
and it’s very bad form to daydream about 
the weekend sports games while a woman 
is trying to get to know you. If this 
becomes a habit, it can be a deal-breaker 
in a relationship. 
2: Coming off as a ‘know-it-all’. When men 
are nervous or insecure, they sometimes 
try too hard to impress. This can manifest 
itself in bragging or even belittling their 
date’s experiences and opinions in order to 
make themselves seem superior. Instead of 
oversharing about your achievements, 
offer little snippets of information to 
create a little intrigue. If your date is 
yawning and checking her phone, it’s a 
sign that you’re talking too much. 
overdoing = doing too much 
turnoff = something that makes 
you lose romantic/sexual interest 
tastefully = appropriately 
accent = call attention to, 
emphasize 
plaster on = apply a liquid or 
cream in great quantity 
space out = get lost in your 
thoughts or simply stop paying 
attention to things around you 
go on autopilot = do habitual 
actions without consciously 
thinking about them 
daydream = letting your mind

that will cause an agreement or

arrogantly displays their 
knowledge 
insecure = not self-confident 
belittling = treat or speak of as 
inferior 
snippets = tiny bits 
yawning = opening her mouth 
wide due to being tired or bored 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
3: Ordering for your date. This is not 
chivalrous, it’s just arrogant – especially 
on a first date when you have little to no 
idea what your female companion likes or 
dislikes. Your date can fend for herself, 
and that includes ordering her own dish. 
4: Asking about sex too soon. Although 
nowadays we are all far less inhibited 
when it comes to talking about what goes 
on between the sheets, don’t jump the 
gun. Early on in a relationship – and 
especially on the first encounter – it’s 
rather sleazy to ask whether a woman 
enjoys a particular sex act or not! 
Communication while dating can also be a 
can of worms. Women often find it 
infuriating how long men can take to 
respond to text messages and how vague 
they can be about plans. Meanwhile, men 
can be hesitant to text or call too much for 
fear of coming on too strong, especially 
early in a relationship when they don’t yet 
know where they stand. 
It simply takes patience and empathy for 
men and women to put up with each 
other’s flaws and have a healthy, mutually 
satisfying relationship.

lessons.title: Poverty Reduction
lessons.fullText:
The Challenge of Reducing Poverty 
Poverty reduction is often at the forefront of 
international discussion, with a plethora of 
government agencies, think tanks, NGOs and 
international institutions laboring to achieve 
this objective.  
Eradicating extreme poverty is one of the 
U.N.’s Millennium Development Goals. The 
aim is to halve both the number of people 
whose income is less than $1 a day and the 
number of people who suffer from hunger. It 
is a noble cause – but how should we go 
about it? 
In spite of a practically universal consensus 
on the need for poverty reduction, there are 
noticeable divergences when it comes to 
concrete proposals to this end. Some of the 
differences stem from the definitions of 
poverty itself, while others are based on 
contrasting opinions about which strategies 
are most effective.  
International institutions such as the United 
Nations, the World Bank and the International 
Monetary Fund (IMF) are engaged in 
defining and measuring global poverty, as 
well as in overseeing programs aimed at 
reducing it, albeit to varying degrees of 
success. There is no quick fix to poverty, 
which is tied to numerous aspects of society 
and everyday life, such as government, 
education, housing, healthcare and income. 
Before proceeding with our analysis, it may 
be useful to clarify some existing definitions 
of poverty. 
at the forefront = in a 
position of importance and 
attention 
a plethora = a large 
number 
laboring = working hard 
eradicating = eliminating 
halve = reduce by half 
a noble cause = a morally 
excellent effort 
go about it = proceed in 
doing it 
stem from = come from 
engaged in = involved and 
active in 
albeit = although, but 
quick fix = simple, fast 
solution 
tied to = connected to 
Vocabulary 


 
 
To start with, the distinction between absolute 
poverty and relative poverty is a potentially 
illuminating one. Absolute poverty measures 
the phenomenon in purely economic terms, by 
assessing whether an individual or a family has 
sufficient financial resources to 
procure 
staples such as food, clothing and shelter. It is 
therefore a somewhat narrow definition in that 
it restricts the criteria to the basic necessities of 
survival, without considering factors such as 
quality of life and societal inequalities.  
The concept of relative poverty addresses some 
of these shortcomings by broadening the 
scope of the definition to account for income 
inequality within societies. It defines poverty 
by assessing a person’s position in society 
relative to the predominant living standards in 
that societal context.  
Both of these definitions of poverty have come 
under fire for placing too much emphasis on 
economic status while overlooking factors 
such 
as 
personal 
and 
community 
empowerment, as well as the extent to which 
people can freely exercise their civic, political 
and social rights.  
Nonetheless, the concepts of absolute and 
relative poverty have been vital to the 
development of poverty-reduction strategies. 
The former has typically been used to measure 
global poverty, and the latter carries more 
weight within specific national contexts.      
In discussing global poverty reduction, one 
topic that often surfaces is the relationship 
between 
the 
developed 
world 
and 
the 
developing world – along with conflicting 
opinions about the nature of this relationship.  
illuminating = something 
that will make things 
clear or help you 
understand 
purely = only 
procure = get 
staples = basic, essential 
items 
narrow = focused and 
specific 
shortcomings = flaws or 
lacks 
broadening = making 
wider or bigger 
predominant = majority, 
strongest 
overlooking = ignoring 
Nonetheless = Still, 
Despite this, or Even so 
vital = essential 
carries more weight = is 
more important or 
applicable 
surfaces = appears, 
comes up in the 
discussion 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
On 
one 
hand, 
Zambian-born 
economist 
Dambisa Moyo has written prolifically about 
how the trillions of dollars that Western 
countries have spent on aid have been 
ineffective in reducing poverty. Instead, she 
argues, this deluge of funds has served to keep 
the African continent in a state of ‘aid 
dependence.’ Moyo advocates free market 
policies 
such 
as 
trade 
and 
financial 
liberalization as being more promising paths to 
economic growth.  
On the other hand, Joseph Stiglitz, former chief 
economist at the World Bank, has highlighted 
the adverse effects of these same free market 
policies and the manner in which they are 
aggressively pushed upon developing nations 
by the IMF and the World Bank. He argues that 
opening up developing financial markets and 
economic sectors to international competition – 
against which they stand little chance of 
success – would be counterproductive. For 
nations whose economies lag behind others’, 
free market policies could actually force them 
further into poverty. 
These are but two examples of diametrically 
opposed views that demonstrate the disparity 
of opinion in poverty reduction debates. It is 
not enough for developed nations to “have 
their heart in the right place” – instead, a 
calculated approach must be taken in order to 
give any aid policy the best chance of success. 
Extensive collaboration with political, local, and 
community leaders in the receiving country is 
also essential to ensure that the aid achieves 
maximum impact. 
    
prolifically = producing a 
lot of work 
advocates = supports, 
argues in favor of 
chief = main, top 
adverse = negative 
pushed upon = forced 
upon or strongly 
encouraged 
counterproductive = 
contrary to the result you 
are trying to achieve 
diametrically opposed = 
completely and directly 
opposite 
have their heart in the 
right place = have good 
intentions 
a calculated approach = 
a careful and analytical 
strategy 
impact = effect 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Notes

• Dambisa Moyo: Dead Aid  
• Joseph Stiglitz: Globalization and its Discontents

lessons.title: Rejection Therapy
lessons.fullText:
Rejection Therapy 
Rejection – the word itself makes us 
cringe. When we’re rejected, we often 
blush, stammer, and feel like a complete 
failure. Rejection stings, and it can be a 
huge blow to our self-esteem. But is it 
possible to turn the tables? One young 
man named Jia Jiang made this his mission. 
 
Jia wanted to be an entrepreneur and 
change the world. He immigrated to the 
United States from China, graduated from 
college, got a stable corporate job, and got 
married. He was a textbook example of a 
success story – but deep down, he felt like 
something was missing. 
 
With his wife’s support and 
encouragement, Jia quit his job to pursue 
his dream of entrepreneurship just a few 
days before the couple’s first baby was 
born. It was a leap of faith, and there was 
a lot at stake.  
 
For four months, Jia worked on the 
prototype of his product and began 
seeking funding. He wanted to succeed so 
badly he dreamt about it five times. 
However, investors ultimately said “no” to 
his venture. There was no explanation and 
no opportunity for discussion.  
 
Jia was crushed. He wanted to keep trying, 
but the fear of experiencing another 
cringe = a physical reaction of 
your body withdrawing or 
shrinking, in reaction to 
something frightening or 
shocking 
blush = when your face turns red 
from embarrassment 
stammer = speak with pauses 
and/or repetitions (often when 
nervous or under a lot of 
pressure) 
stings = hurts with a sharp pain 
a huge blow to = something that 
damages 
a textbook example = a perfect, 
typical example 
deep down = secretly in his 
thoughts and feelings 
a leap of faith = a risk, believing 
things would somehow be 
successful 
prototype = first model of a 
product (before production) 
crushed = completely sad and 
depressed  
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
rejection had paralyzed him. This prompted Jia 
to search online for ways to overcome it – and 
he came across something called “Rejection 
Therapy.” This is the idea that experiencing 
repeated rejections can help you become 
tougher.  
 
Jia decided to make 100 deliberate attempts to 
get rejected over the course of 100 days. He 
posted videos and write-ups on his blog so that 
he could be publicly accountable for 
completing the challenge. 
 
Some of the tasks he chose seemed silly – like 
asking for a free “burger refill” at a fast-food 
restaurant, or dancing in front of a security 
camera. Others were bound to create awkward 
social situations, such as joining a complete 
stranger’s party or asking passers-by to rate his 
looks on a scale from 1 to 10. And a few really 
took guts, like his requests to feed a lion, fly a 
plane with no experience, and interview 
President Obama. 
  
As Jia diligently tried task after task, he began 
to view the concept of rejection differently. It 
occurred to him that President Obama won the 
election with 51% of the vote – but that 49% of 
the votes had been against him. Jia began to 
ponder how various people dealt with rejection 
without being crippled by fear. Each time Jia set 
out to do a new challenge, he would brace 
himself for the rejection – but the results were 
surprising even to him. 
 
paralyzed = made it so that 
he could not take action 
prompted = motivated, 
caused 
tougher = less sensitive; 
able to experience great 
pressure without breaking 
deliberate = on purpose 
accountable = expected to 
do what he said he would 
passers-by = people walking 
by in a public place 
diligently = with consistent 
effort and perseverance 
It occurred to him = he 
realized; the idea came into 
his mind 
ponder = think deeply 
about 
crippled = physically or (in 
this case) emotionally 
unable to move or walk 
brace himself = prepare 
mentally and physically for 
pain or for an impact 
 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Amidst a sea of ‘no’s’, there were a few people 
who said ‘yes’. When Jia knocked on the door 
of a random stranger to ask if he could play 
soccer in his backyard, the gentleman said 
‘come on in!’ Jia asked to drive a police car as 
if he were a cop – and the officer let him do it.  
 
One of the most remarkable experiences was 
when he went into a donut shop and made a 
special request to have donuts customized to 
look like the Olympic rings. The manager, 
Jackie, painstakingly created the set of 
donuts for him – and then said that they were 
on the house.  
 
Jia began to realize that there were many 
people who would agree even to a seemingly 
preposterous request. There was a human 
element that transcended the experience, 
providing small glitters of hope throughout 
the 100 days. Instead of dwelling on the 
rejections, Jia began to revel in the ‘yes 
moments.’  His fear of being rejected was 
superseded by the hope of finding the next 
open-minded stranger who would say “yes.”  
 
After his video of the donut incident went 
viral, Jia began receiving e-mails from fans 
who were inspired by his courage. By sharing 
his story, he has now become a successful 
public speaker. His quest to overcome 
rejection ended up jump-starting his career, 
enabling him to achieve his dream of changing 
the world.

lessons.title: Seven Unusual Hotels
lessons.fullText:
Seven Unusual Hotels 
You could always go to a regular old hotel, stay in 
a nice clean room, and eat generic food in their 
dining room… but what if you want something a 
bit more memorable? 
There are hundreds of unique hotels in the world, 
but in the interests of keeping things concise, 
here are seven that caught my eye. 
1. Hotel Kakslauttanen in Finland 
If you’ve ever seen the northern lights, you 
know that they’re breathtaking. Now, 
imagine seeing them from inside a 
transparent igloo. 
The Hotel Kakslauttanen is located in 
northern Finland, and believe it or not, all 
the cabins are made out of ice, or glass that 
looks like ice. They offer a great view, but 
needless to say not a whole lot of privacy.  
2. Jules’s Undersea Lodge in Florida 
This was once a research laboratory, and 
has been repurposed as an underwater 
hotel that’s actually located on the bottom 
of Florida’s Emerald Lagoon. Checking in 
memorable = remarkable 
and worth remembering 
concise = short, expressed 
in few words 
breathtaking = amazing 
(usually describes an 
amazing sight or view) 
igloo = a round building 
usually constructed with 
blocks of snow or ice 
believe it or not = it might 
seem hard to believe, but 
it’s true 
repurposed = changed and 
adapted to serve a 
different purpose 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
could be a bit of a problem if you’re not 
adventurous – you have to scuba dive six 
meters down to get to the hotel. 
3. Das Park Hotel in Austria 
The rooms in this hotel are built inside 
concrete sewer pipes on the banks of the 
Danube River. Each pipe segment is 2.5 
meters long, 2 meters in diameter, and 
boasts comfy futons with blankets. And it 
won’t cost you an arm and a leg – the 
guests actually determine the rates. 
4. Dog Bark Park in Idaho 
It’s referred to as the world’s largest 
beagle. This hotel is built in the shape of a 
huge dog, nine meters long. A room 
contains a queen size bed along with two 
twin mattresses in the loft. You’ll get dog-
shaped cookies, too! Everything is dog-
themed. Oddly enough, though, you can’t 
bring pets without prior approval. It’s 
relatively inexpensive - $98 per night for 
double occupancy. 
5. 1950s Bristol Fighter Plane in New 
Zealand

and oxygen tank

Vocabulary 


 
 
This tiny little two-room hotel is made from 
one of the last planes out of Vietnam. It sleeps 
four in the body of the plane, and four in the 
cockpit. It’s not expensive, but you’d better 
book early, because space is limited! 
6. Kadir’s Tree Houses in Turkey 
On Turkey’s island of Olimpos, you can stay in a 
little wooden bungalow that is nestled in the 
trees. Kadir’s offers over a hundred such 
bungalows, and is known as a great party spot. 
Would you believe that you can stay there for 
just $20 per night? 
7. Kokopelli’s Cave Bed & Breakfast in New 
Mexico 
You might think that sleeping in a cave isn’t 
luxurious – but you’d be wrong. At Kokopelli’s, 
you can stay in a fully-furnished room that’s 
dug into an ancient sandstone cliff. Your room 
will be carpeted and have all the creature 
comforts you’d expect, and you can stay there 
for just $280 per night. 
So if you’re looking for an interesting experience for 
your next vacation, consider staying at these one-of-
a-kind hotels – you’ll certainly never forget your stay!

lessons.title: Shipwrecks
lessons.fullText:
Three Fascinating Shipwrecks 
 
There is something about a shipwreck 
that captivates us. We wonder what led 
to the ship’s demise, and envision 
everything from pirates to espionage. 
The United Nations estimates that there 
are around three million shipwrecks 
littering the ocean floors. Here are a few 
of the interesting stories behind them: 
 
The American Star 
 
The American Star was built in 1940 and 
was used to transport both troops and 
civilians for 25 years. The vessel then 
changed hands many times, eventually 
falling into disrepair after years of 
neglect. It was sold for scrapping in the 
1980s, but a company purchased it with 
the intention of converting it into a five-
star hotel.  
 
However, while the American Star was 
being towed, a thunderstorm caused it 
to run aground in the Canary Islands. 
The strong waves pummeled the ship so 
forcefully that it broke in two, and the 
American Star was written off as a total 
loss and abandoned. Over the next 
fourteen years, the wreck slowly 
succumbed to the sea and now nothing 
remains but a few pieces of twisted steel.

and holds our attention 
demise = death or termination 
envision = imagine 
espionage = the practice of spying 
littering = scattered in various 
places 
troops = soldiers 
civilians = non-military people 
vessel = ship 
changed hands = was bought/sold 
or given 
scrapping = being taken apart so 
that the parts and metal can be 
used for other things

vehicle

strongly 
written off = dropped from 
consideration

Vocabulary 


 
 
The “Black Swan Project” 
 
Odyssey Marine Exploration is an American 
company that salvages valuable items from deep-
water shipwrecks. In 2007, they hit the jackpot 
with the discovery of a wreck off the coast of 
Portugal containing gold and silver coins estimated 
at $500 million. Odyssey code-named the operation 
“the Black Swan Project” and remained secretive 
about the exact location of the dive site. 
 
The treasure was initially thought to be from the 
English ship Merchant Royal, which sank in 1641 
with a heavy cargo of silver and gold. But the 
Spanish government disputed this, claiming that 
the wreck was actually a Spanish vessel called 
Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes. This ship was 
bringing treasure from South America to Spain 
when it was intercepted by the British and sunk 
during the ensuing battle. 
 
This caused a lengthy legal battle in American 
courts, during which the coins were closely 
examined and Odyssey was forced to disclose the 
location of the wreck. It was finally determined that 
the shipwreck and its treasure rightfully belonged 
to Spain. The coins were transported to Alicante, 
where they are now on display at a museum. 
 
Andrea Doria  
 
Italy's Andrea Doria, launched in 1951, was hailed 
as one of the safest and most beautiful vessels ever 
built. It had a double hull, watertight 
compartments, plenty of lifeboats, and early-
salvages = rescues 
objects from a 
destroyed area 
cargo = the objects 
being carried and 
transported by a ship, 
plane, or truck 
intercepted = stopped 
while in motion 
ensuing = what 
happened afterwards or 
as a result 
lengthy = long 
hull = the exterior of a 
ship 
lifeboats = small boats 
to be used in case of 
emergency 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
warning radar technology. It was also quite 
luxurious, being adorned with over $1 million in 
art and décor. 
 
On July 25, 1956, the Andrea Doria was 
approaching New York on a foggy night. Another 
ship, called the Stockholm, was departing. 
Misinterpretation of radar signals and poor 
visibility created a recipe for disaster, and the two 
ships collided. 
 
Fortunately, the Andrea Doria's safety features 
enabled it to stay above water long enough for 
1,663 people on board to be rescued (57 died as a 
direct result of the collision). The ship took a full 11 
hours to sink, and the world watched the whole 
situation unfold on live TV. After this disaster, 
flying became the preferred method of trans-
Atlantic travel. 
 
The shipwreck itself is known as "the Mount 
Everest of scuba diving," since the hazardous 
conditions require immense skill and experience 
to navigate. There are strong currents and an 
invisible web of thin fishing lines that can ensnare 
divers, sixteen of whom have lost their lives while 
exploring the wreck.

to describe the interior

lessons.fullText:
6 Songs that Changed 
the World 
They say music is the universal language.  It 
speaks to us. It moves us. It gets our feet 
tapping, it makes us dance, and it makes us cry.  
Occasionally a song comes along that's so 
powerful that it changes the very world we live 
in. Maybe it inspires social change or helps us 
relate to the plight of our fellow man. One song 
with a striking message can bring home a 
point even better than a speech or rally.   
Keep reading to discover six songs that have 
packed a punch in the past century. 
“I Wanna Hold Your Hand” by 
The Beatles 
This is the song that kick-started "Beatlemania" 
in the United States. After it aired, there was a 
landslide of purchases of the hit single. The 
upbeat song was a godsend to a nation that was 
still reeling from the assassination of President 
John F. Kennedy one month prior.  
“Johnny B. Goode” by Chuck 
Berry 
Many consider Chuck Berry to be the father of 
modern rock n' roll – and this is his crown 
jewel. Music today just wouldn't be the same 
without this one.  
Magazines like “The Rolling Stone” have called it 
the best guitar track ever – and NASA even sent 
a recording of it in the Voyager spacecraft. The 
tapping = touching the floor 
on and off and making a noise 
plight = a bad or unfortunate 
situation 
striking = describes something 
that gets your attention, or is 
shocking or surprising 
bring home a point = make 
the point clear and make you 
truly feel its truth 
rally = gathering of people in 
support of a cause or to 
protest something 
packed a punch = had a 
significant impact 
aired = was broadcast on TV 
or radio 
a landslide of = a HUGE 
number/amount of 
upbeat = cheerful 
a godsend = something 
wanted or needed that 
appears unexpectedly 
crown jewel = the most 
valuable thing in a group 
spacecraft = a vehicle that 
leaves the planet 
Vocabulary 


 
 
funny thing is that the track itself is about a man 
who's great at playing guitar.  
 “A Change is Gonna Come” by 
Sam Cooke 
This song, released in 1964, tells a story of a man 
who's convinced that things will change soon – 
for the better. It was inspired by Cooke's own 
experiences with discrimination and 
segregation – particularly an incident where he 
and his wife were turned away from a “whites-
only” motel in the southern U.S. 
The sad yet prophetic tune resonated with 
audiences in the '60s and became the anthem for 
the American Civil Rights Movement.  
“Imagine” by John Lennon 
Lennon's most successful solo effort asks us to 
picture a world without religion, borders, or 
violence. Both the utopic vision and the 
soothing melody struck a chord with listeners, 
and it's been considered one of the greatest 
songs of all time ever since.  
In an interview, Lennon admitted that his anti-
religious, anti-capitalistic, anti-nationalistic 
message was contentious – but said that

SpaceX and Its Plan to 
Colonize Mars 
Have you ever said to yourself, “I’d just love to 
get away from it all”? Well, how about going to 
Mars? Seriously. Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, 
is aiming to colonize Mars by 2026.  
SpaceX has actually made significant strides 
toward putting humans on the red planet. Elon 
Musk’s goal is for humankind to become a 
multi-planet species so that we can survive 
even a catastrophic event on earth. If you 
spend a few minutes perusing the recent 
achievements of SpaceX, you have to believe 
that it might just be possible. 
The problem with rocket ships is that they cost 
a pretty penny to build and can’t easily be 
reused. However, SpaceX was able to send a 
rocket to replenish supplies at the International 
Space Station, then return it to earth – becoming 
the first private company to do so. SpaceX now 
has a $1.6 billion contract with NASA to deliver 
cargo to the space station, as well as many other 
customers vying for its services. 
Running errands is not the long-term goal for 
SpaceX, though. The company is working

people in a new area

general 
species = type/category of 
living thing

considering

lot of money

replenish = provide more 
supplies when the first

Vocabulary 


 
 
towards making rocket travel 100 times more 
affordable – which, if achieved, would be a game-
changer for space travel. 
SpaceX is planning a manned mission to the red 
planet in the very near future.  There are significant 
technological hurdles to be overcome, but Musk is 
dead-set on making it possible – and he’s putting 
his money where his mouth is.  
Elon Musk, who is originally from South Africa, sold 
his start-up software company Zip2 for $300 million 
when he was only 28 years old. This was just 
peanuts compared to when his next company, 
PayPal, was sold to eBay for $1.5 billion. After 
dabbling in a hedonistic lifestyle, Musk quickly 
realized that he needed a more meaningful project 
to sink his teeth into. He began pouring his energy 
and fortune into a couple of incredibly ambitious 
start-ups.  
First he founded Tesla, which aims to replace all the 
cars in the world with electric vehicles (the change 
is already underway). Then came SpaceX, which he 
formed in 2002 and funded with $100M of his own 
money. 
Although 
both

Vocabulary 


 
 
If you’d asked people centuries ago if it would be 
possible to colonize the “New World,” meaning the 
United States and Canada, they might have told you 
that the journey was impossible, the landscape was 
brutal, and the possibility of survival slim to none. 
Think about how far we’ve come as a civilization. 
One thing is for sure – if we ever do colonize other 
planets, it will be visionaries like Elon Musk who 
will make it possible.

lessons.title: Strange Sports
lessons.fullText:
Four Strange Sports  
from Around the World 
Because sports like soccer and volleyball are 
well-known around the world, it’s easy to forget 
that there are hundreds of lesser-known sports 
that are only played and followed by the most 
devoted fans.  
Some of these sports come from ancient 
cultural traditions, while others are very new – 
often the combination of two or more sports 
you may already know. Here are a few weird 
sports you might never have heard of.  
Underwater Hockey 
According to CMAS.org, this unusual sport was 
invented by the British Navy in the 1950s as a 
type of training exercise for divers.  
The game is played with ten to twelve players 
per team, and in contrast to the array of pads 
in a normal hockey game, each swimmer only 
has a diving mask and snorkel, large fins, and a 
thick glove.  
ancient = very old 
weird = strange, unusual 
Navy = the part of the 
military that operates on 
the ocean, with ships and 
submarines 
divers = people who 
explore underwater 
pads = soft cushions that 
protect from impact 
snorkel = tube for 
breathing outside the 
water 
fins = rubber or plastic 
“shoes” used for 
swimming underwater  
Vocabulary 


 
 
The game is played with a heavy lead puck that 
sinks to the bottom of the pool, and players must 
constantly resurface and then dive again while 
keeping track of the puck and other players’ 
movements. Like normal ice or field hockey, the 
teams try to score by passing the puck through 
the goal of the other team. 
Dog Dancing 
Dog dancing, or canine freestyle, is one of the 
most unique and mesmerizing sports you could 
watch. According to MusicalDogSport.org, it 
combines training, cooperation, and music to 
create a choreographed dance between a dog 
and owner.  
Each dance is meant to be representative of a 
dog’s inner personality and its relationship with 
its loving owner. In this sport, teams of dogs and 
owners compete against each other, and the 
teams that receive the best scores win. 
Eukonkanto 
Eukonkanto, which translates to “wife-carrying” 
in English, is a tongue-in-cheek Finnish sport 
that is starting to develop a worldwide following 
due to its hilarious visuals.  
lead = a type of metal 
puck = the round black 
object used in hockey 
games 
resurface = come back up 
to the surface 
mesmerizing = something 
that keeps your close 
attention 
choreographed = the 
movements were planned 
in advance 
tongue-in-cheek = 
expressed ironically 
Finnish = from Finland 
hilarious = very funny 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
The sport is an obstacle course-style race. Men 
must race each other through different types of 
terrain such as sand, gravel, or water. Some 
Eukonkanto events are longer distances while 
others are more like short sprints.  
The catch is that each man must carry a woman 
on his back for the entire race – hence the name, 
“wife-carrying.” The women agree to do this 
willingly. 
Chess Boxing 
This sport is exactly what it sounds like: two 
competitors compete in eleven rounds of chess 
and boxing, alternating between the activities 
after each round. A winner is declared after either 
a boxing stoppage or checkmate.  
If there is no winner after eleven rounds, the 
fighter with the most points from the boxing 
rounds will be declared the winner. The fighters 
also have an agreed-upon time for each chess 
round, so if one person is taking too much time to 
make his moves, he might lose the match due to a 
time penalty. 
…………………

with various physical 
obstacles and difficulties 
gravel = small rocks 
sprint = a short, quick 
burst of speed 
willingly = voluntarily 
(they agree to do it; 
nobody is forcing them) 
rounds = the different 
“sections” of a 
competition or game 
show 
checkmate = when one 
chess player traps the 
other, and wins the game 
Vocabulary 


 
 
So, what did you think of these four non-traditional sports? If they sound interesting, 
you might want to give them a shot. You never know if one could become your new 
favorite hobby!

• http://www.eukonkanto.fi/en/ 
• http://worldchessboxing.com/

lessons.title: Fame After 40
lessons.fullText:
Fame After 40 
 
Some people moan about their 40th 
birthdays as if their best years were behind 
them. But there are a significant number of 
famous and successful people who didn’t 
really come into their own until their 40s, 
50s, or even older.  
 
If you’re turning 40 – or if you’ve already 
passed that milestone – don’t despair! You 
could be on the cusp of an exciting new 
chapter in life. Let’s learn about a few 
phenomenal achievements made by folks 
over 40. 
 
Stan Lee 
Everyone knows Spiderman and the X-Men 
– but how much do you know about the 
man who came up with these legendary 
characters? Stan Lee penned his first hit 
comic book when he was just shy of his 
39th birthday. He had already been in the 
comics business for twenty years, and 
although he had a knack for writing, none 
of his comics had caught on.  
come into their own = finally get 
recognition and success 
 
milestone = a point or mark of 
significant progress on a journey 
or in a process 
 
despair = become very sad and 
hopeless 
 
on the cusp of = at a point in 
time that marks the beginning of 
 
phenomenal = incredibly great 
 
folks = people (informal) 
 
penned = wrote 
 
hit = successful (informal) 
 
just shy of = just before 
 
had a knack for = had natural 
skill in 
 
caught on = become popular 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
At the time, he was thinking of quitting the 
business entirely, so he had nothing to lose – 
and he decided to experiment with a new 
approach, creating superheroes with complex 
personalities and flaws. This group of 
characters – the Fantastic Four – catapulted 
Lee to success and led to the creation of the 
entire Marvel Universe. Today, Lee is in his 90s 
and continues to make cameo appearances in 
films. 
 
Henry Ford  
The car is a ubiquitous part of our daily life – 
and the man who invented it spent fifteen years 
on its development. Ford came from a family of 
farmers, but he despised farm work and 
became an engineer instead. With backing 
from investors, Ford successfully created a self-
propelled vehicle – but this revolutionary 
invention was not popular right off the bat.  
 
The landmark Model T was launched in 1908, 
when Ford was 45 years old. He fervently 
promoted the car in newspapers and through a 
network of independent dealers, and by 1918, 
half the cars in America were Model Ts. 
had nothing to lose = there 
were no negative 
consequences to taking a 
risk 
 
catapulted Lee to success = 
made him successful very 
quickly 
 
cameo appearances = a brief 
appearance in a very small 
part of a movie 
 
ubiquitous = appearing to be 
everywhere 
 
backing = support 
 
right off the bat = 
immediately 
 
fervently = intensely and 
passionately 
 
dealers = people who sell 
something produced by 
others 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Charles Darwin  
Darwin is one of the most influential figures in 
scientific history. He was passionate about 
natural science and mostly kept to himself, 
devoting years to his research on wildlife and 
fossils. Mired in work and under pressure 
from his publisher to deliver, Darwin 
developed myriad health problems. Despite 
this, he was able to put the finishing touches 
on his theory of natural selection, and his 
landmark work, "On the Origin of Species," 
was published when he was 50 years old. 
 
Julia Child  
She is one of the most famous celebrity chefs, 
renowned for making the art of French 
cooking accessible to the American public. 
However, she wasn’t always a culinary 
virtuoso – her early career was spent in 
advertising, and she also did a stint in the 
military as a research assistant. Her husband 
introduced her to fine French cuisine, and she 
later studied cooking in Paris. Child’s 726-page 
masterpiece, "Mastering the Art of French 
Cooking," was published in 1961, when she was 
49 years old. She went on to star in multiple 
kept to himself = was 
introverted; didn’t have 
much contact with other 
people 
 
wildlife = animals in nature 
 
fossils = skeletons of 
plants/animals that are 
preserved in rock 
 
mired in work = having a 
LOT of work; too much to 
handle 
 
myriad = many and various 
 
put the finishing touches on 
= finally finish the last details 
 
landmark = important in 
history

lessons.title: The Origins of Disney
lessons.fullText:
The Origins of Disney 
You probably thought it all began with a mouse, 
didn’t you? Mickey Mouse has been the face of 
Disney for nearly a century, after the cartoon 
that brought him into the spotlight in 1928. 
Some even remember that Mickey was originally 
called “Mortimer.” 
It takes a real Disney maven to know that it 
actually began with a rabbit. Walt Disney’s first 
series of animated films featured Oswald, the 
Lucky Rabbit. It was Walt’s wife who thought that 
a mouse might be more appealing, and she 
encouraged Walt to pull back, regroup, and think 
about a mouse. 
The rest is history. 
The 1930s and 1940s 
In 1929, Walt Disney formed Walt Disney 
Productions and released a number of cartoons 
starring Mickey Mouse. Later on, he added the 
lovably irascible Donald Duck, as well as Goofy 
and Pluto. When it came to animation, Disney 
quite simply dominated the market.

position of fame and 
prominence

interest

used for an actor or 
character appearing in a 
film, TV show, or 
performance)

outbursts of anger

controlled, was the 
strongest in the area 
 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Then, Walt got an idea – what if cartoons could 
actually be full-length feature films? In 1937, he 
began creating his vision of the fairy tale, “Snow 
White and the Seven Dwarfs.” He obviously didn’t 
know that the correct plural of “dwarf” is 
“dwarves,” but who cares? It was a resounding 
success. 
Walt Disney productions followed Snow White 
with a complex take on the story of Pinocchio, 
instilling terror into the hearts of children (and 
maybe a few adults) worldwide with the 
portrayal of Monstro, the whale. In addition to 
being a cinematic coup, it was a tale of the 
triumph of good over evil.  
Some would say that this was a parallel to the 
innocent nature of Walt Disney himself, who 
always wanted to see good prevail. Over the past 
few decades, more information has come to light 
about Walt Disney being a horrible boss and a 
homophobe. Yet there was an innocence about 
the man that came through in his animated 
movies. 
Walt was a perfectionist, and cared deeply about 
the quality of his productions. Despite founding 
one of the richest empires in the history of TV 
and film, Walt Disney lived very modestly. He

The 1950s and Beyond 
In the mid-20th century, the company flourished 
with television shows like “The Mickey Mouse 
Club,” “The Wonderful World of Disney,” and 
“Walt Disney Presents.” Disney continued to 
adapt beloved stories and fairy tales like 
Sleeping Beauty, Cinderella, and Winnie the Pooh.  
In the 1970s and 1980s, it looked for a while as 
though Disney was floundering. But Ron Miller, 
Walt’s son-in-law, had a daring idea: to develop 
films that would appeal to an older audience. The 
expansion of the target market was successful, as 
Disney produced several films that were hits 
with teens and adults.  
Yes, and More! 
Today, Disney is an entertainment empire. Its 
theme parks delight children of all ages, all over 
the world. Disney brands them as the happiest 
places on earth, and they might be right. There’s 
even a Disney cruise line. Where will it go from 
here? Who knows? The sky’s the limit!

lessons.title: The Psychology of Advertising
lessons.fullText:
The Psychology of Advertising 
 
The psychology of advertising goes beyond 
just a catchy tune and colorful product 
packaging. It taps into the area of the brain 
where humans can be influenced without 
being cognizant of the fact that we’re being 
persuaded.  
 
The visual aspects are the most prevalent – 
for example, the subtle placement of 
attractive young women in the background 
of a product for men, or the slanted ‘e’s in 
the Heineken beer logo that simulate a 
smile. These advertisements are 
meticulously engineered to 
subconsciously hook you and make you 
want the products.  
 
In the book entitled Hidden Persuasions, 
Marc Andrews, a psychologist and creative 
director from Amsterdam, works with two 
social psychologists to pry into many of the 
psychological ploys that are used in 
advertising. Marketing gurus design 
advertisements not only to plug the 
benefits of the product itself, but also to 
evoke an emotional response. The goal is to 
make consumers want the item so badly 
that the product goes from a “want” to a 
“need.” 
 
One of the most popular ways to create an 
emotional connection is through 
a catchy tune = melody of a 
song that is appealing and easy 
to remember 
cognizant = aware 
subtle = difficult to notice; not 
obvious 
slanted = inclined 
logo = a symbol or graphic that 
represents a company 
simulate = take on the 
appearance of 
meticulously engineered = 
carefully created and developed 
hook = catch your attention 
pry into = investigate or inquire 
closely 
ploys = clever and potentially 
deceptive ways to achieve a 
goal 
evoke = give rise to, produce 
want something badly = want it 
very much 
Vocabulary 


 
 
anthropomorphism – altering a common 
object so that it appears to be more human-
like.  We have all seen examples of this in 
television commercials that feature 
everything from dancing laundry detergent 
to talking cereal. Although such tactics 
might seem silly, they are designed to help 
us bond with the brand or product, making 
us more likely to buy it. 
 
Another strategy involves linking a product 
with something intangible that we all 
yearn for. A washing machine, for example, 
can be presented as not just an appliance – 
but instead, as an integral part of caring for 
one’s family. Although you might not be 
immediately prompted to buy a washing 
machine by such a commercial, the 
associations linger in your mind when it’s 
time to make a buying decision. 
 
Our desire for social acceptance represents 
another vulnerability for advertisers to 
exploit. When phrases like “9 out of 10 
people prefer this product” or “1 million 
happy customers” are used, this triggers 
both our longing to be part of a group and 
our fear of being the odd one out. Although 
we might pride ourselves on our 
individuality, social proof in advertising 
actually makes us more likely to jump on 
the bandwagon. 
 
Advertisers also make use of reverse 
psychology. The trick is to appeal to the side 
of human nature that has an aversion to 
altering = changing 
silly = ridiculous, funny 
bond with = make a strong 
emotional connection with 
intangible = non-physical, not 
able to be touched 
yearn for = strongly and deeply 
desire 
integral = essential 
prompted = caused 
vulnerability = point of 
weakness or openness 
exploit = take advantage of in a 
way that may cause harm 
triggers = activates 
longing = desire 
the odd one out = the person 
who is clearly different from 
others and viewed as strange 
aversion = dislike or desire to 
avoid 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
being persuaded. The advertisement will 
not use hype, nor will it put down its 
competitors – instead it will simply mention 
them and leave the decision to the 
consumer. This method endears people to 
the brand because they feel their intellect 
and objectivity have been respected. 
 
Each of these tricks is part of the game of 
advertising psychology – and marketing 
professionals have many more tactics up 
their sleeve. In fact, they usually design 
various versions of an advertisement, then 
run trials with groups of people in order to 
hone the messaging and gauge which 
version is most effective.  
 
Make a mental note of these strategies and 
see if you can spot them in the ads you see 
every day.

presentation that makes

really is

inferior

remember

briefly or see something that is 
hard to observe/find

lessons.fullText:
What’s the Deal with Tipping? 
 
Tipping service workers is a common practice in 
certain American industries. It is a way to show 
appreciation – or, for that matter, express your 
grievances – with the quality of service. There is 
some controversy over whether or not to tip, 
and although tipping is supposedly voluntary, 
the social pressure makes it feel like a must.  
 
The custom of tipping arose shortly after the 
Civil War, and was adopted from Europe. 
Americans with the means to travel abroad 
brought the ritual back with them, and flaunted 
the habit to demonstrate their status. Tipping 
was initially looked down upon as inconsistent 
with an egalitarian society. But in the early 20th 
century, the prohibition on alcoholic beverages 
caused hotels and restaurants to lose revenue, 
and proprietors began to welcome tips from 
customers.  
 
The most common setting for tips is in 
restaurants, where diners typically add an extra 
fifteen to twenty percent of the total bill as 
gratuity. The reason for such a sizeable tip is 
because waiters and waitresses often earn a 
pittance – they make far less than minimum 
wage; sometimes as low as just a couple dollars 
an hour. The workers are therefore banking on 
receiving tips in order to make a decent living. 
 
Some Americans begrudge being expected to 
pay a tip on top of the established price. This is 
grievances = complaints 
 
a must = an obligation, 
something you have to do 
 
Civil War = a “civil war” 
refers to a war inside one 
country. The American Civil 
War happened in the 1860s 
 
flaunted = showed off, 
arrogantly made sure 
everyone could see it  
 
egalitarian = characterized 
by equality 
 
proprietors = owners 
 
gratuity = another word for 
“tip” 
 
a pittance = an insultingly 
small amount of money 
 
begrudge = are reluctant to 
accept 
  
Vocabulary 


 
 
especially the case when restaurants mandate 
tips for larger parties (often groups of six or 
more), and tack on the cost of the tip in the final 
bill. Those who resent the practice of tipping say 
it should be the responsibility of the restaurant 
owner—not the patrons—to compensate the 
staff fairly.  
 
In Europe, where the practice of tipping 
originated, waiters are paid higher wages and 
receive only small tips, such as leftover change – 
not to contribute to the bulk of their income, 
but simply as a gesture of goodwill. However, in 
these countries, the cost of employing waiters is 
built into the cost of the food.  
 
If tips were abolished in the U.S., the prices on 
the menu would have to rise in order to 
compensate for the costlier payroll – likely 
causing the restaurant to lose customers. 
Tipping is so entrenched in American culture 
that few restaurant owners are willing to stick 
their necks out. 
 
There is, however, an experimental movement of 
no-tip restaurants. Girard, a French restaurant in 
Philadelphia, prohibits tipping and pays its 
servers thirteen dollars an hour (more than 
twice minimum wage). The owners admit they 
forfeit some personal income to maintain this 
policy, but they are adamant that it pays off in 
terms of a better atmosphere for both diners and 
servers.  
 
Other professions for which receiving tips is the 
norm in the U.S. include hairdressers, 
mandate = command,

Famous Unsolved 
Crimes 
The problems of crime and violence are as old 
as humanity itself. Although we now have the 
help of cutting-edge technology to identify the 
perpetrators and bring them to justice, some 
crimes remain unsolved. 
 
Jack the Ripper 
 
The people of London lived in fear and 
anguish during Jack the Ripper’s murderous 
rampage in 1888. The prostitutes working the 
streets in the seedy areas of the city often had 
no other recourse for supporting themselves, 
thus making them easy prey. Between August 
7th and November 10th, 1888, five women were 
found not only murdered, but also horribly 
maimed, having been slashed with a knife.    
 
There was a sadistic serial killer at large – 
one who even sent handwritten notes to the 
police, taunting them. The investigators 
believed that the killer was well-versed in 
some form of medical surgery, based on the 
removal of organs and overall cutting process.

committed a crime

suffering

violent, or destructive 
behavior

bad or dangerous

or thing for help or 
protection 
maimed = body very badly 
injured / damaged 
slashed = cut in a violent way 
sadistic = describes someone 
who enjoys inflicting pain 
at large = not yet captured 
taunting = teasing or 
provoking 
well-versed = very 
knowledgeable and skilled in

Potential leads were brought to the attention of 
London’s police brigade, but there was not 
enough proof to convict any of the suspects.  
After the string of murders ceased, the case 
eventually faded from the public eye. To this 
day, it remains one of the world’s most popular 
unsolved cases. 
The Beaumont Children 
 
One of Australia's most infamous cold cases is 
that of the Beaumont children, who seemingly 
vanished into thin air. On January 26, 1966, three 
siblings, ages nine, seven, and four went to a 
beach that they visited often. In that era, it was 
common and safe for young children to play 
unsupervised. The normally mature and reliable 
Beaumont children were expected to be home by 
noon – yet they never returned. 
 
Witnesses reported the presence of a tall, thin 
blonde man playing with the children on the 
beach, and the children seemed to be at ease with 
him. The oldest sister was then spotted buying a 
snack with money her mother had not given her. 
At around 3 PM, the mail carrier saw the children

The Gardner Museum Heist 
 
The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston is

in a simple yet clever robbery, making it the United 
States’ largest ever theft of private property.

The FBI has been unable to crack the case

Unfortunately, none of the stolen masterpieces

lessons.title: History of US-Cuba Relations
lessons.fullText:
History of  
U.S.-Cuba Relations 
In December 2014, President Obama announced the 
decision to reopen diplomatic and economic relations 
with Cuba. Diplomatic ties had been officially severed 
for decades, and the relationship of the U.S. and Cuba 
has a long and confusing history. Through eleven 
presidencies, Americans have watched the country’s 
relationship with Cuba worsen, as both sides have 
been reluctant to make concessions to the other. 
The Beginning 
Fidel Castro first took power in Cuba in 1959. Later 
that year, he visited the United States and met with 
Vice President Nixon. At this time, both countries were 
still establishing their diplomatic relationship, but the 
American government was wary of some of Castro’s 
communistic rhetoric. 
Things took a decisive turn in 1960 when Castro not 
only continued to strengthen his relationship with the 
Soviet Union, but also nationalized all American 
companies in Cuba and provided no compensation. It 
was at this time that the U.S. cut relations and imposed 
the first trade embargo on Cuba.

relationships

presidencies = time 
periods of each 
president 
make concessions = 
give the other side 
something it wants 
wary = cautious, 
slightly suspicious 
rhetoric = 
communication

decisive turn = things 
began clearly going in 
a particular direction

them the property of 
the national 
government 
trade embargo = a 
barrier to importing 
or exporting to/from 
that country 
Vocabulary 


 
 
The Bay of Pigs 
In 1961, President Kennedy approved the Bay of Pigs 
mission where the U.S. government supported an 
attempted invasion by Cuban exiles. Fidel Castro 
easily defeated the U.S.-backed army and began more 
openly supporting the Soviet Union. This became only 
the first of eight U.S. attempts in the 1960s to oust 
Castro. Each obviously ended in failure. 
The Cuban Missile Crisis 
In 1962, Cuba and the Soviet Union agreed to house 
Soviet nuclear missiles on the island. The U.S. released 
photos of the missile silos and began an international 
standoff with the Soviet Union. Though many feared a 
nuclear war would begin, both sides were able to 
deescalate the situation by agreeing to remove the 
Soviet missiles in Cuba and the U.S. missiles in Turkey. 
Mariel Boatlift 
When the U.S. government said that it would welcome 
Cuban refugees, it resulted in the Mariel boatlift of 
1980. This was the largest arrival of Cuban refugees at 
one time, as approximately 125,000 people arrived on 
American shores. It is suspected that many of these 
people were individuals who Castro willingly freed 
from his prisons and mental institutions in order to

Vocabulary

Wet Foot, Dry Foot 
Eventually the U.S. government adopted the “wet foot, 
dry foot” policy, which indicated that if refugees 
arrived on U.S. soil, they could stay. Refugees that 
were caught before they reached the shore were sent 
back. 
Various changes to refugee policies, cultural exchange, 
and remittances have been made in the last twenty 
years. Despite all these tweaks, the situation remained 
the same as it has for over four decades.  
President Obama’s decision ushers in a new age for 
U.S.-Cuba relations. This could mean greater cultural 
and economic exchange as well as the improvement of 
lives for the poorest in Cuba. However, it is still too 
early to tell.

lessons.title: Vaccines
lessons.fullText:
Vaccines 
 
Vaccines are invaluable in helping humanity 
fight disease. They help us prevent illness 
rather than just treating after transmission. 
In fact, according to the Centers for Disease 
Control, vaccines are the most effective 
means of preempting infectious diseases and 
stopping outbreaks in their tracks.  
 
Vaccines work by introducing a weakened or 
dead form of a disease into a person’s body. 
The body’s immune system reacts by creating 
antibodies to fight even the mild presence of 
the infection. Then, if the person ever catches 
the full-fledged infection, the body’s 
defenses are already equipped to attack and 
destroy it. 
 
The theory behind vaccines was first applied 
by an Englishman named Edward Jenner in 
the 1760s. He heard that dairy farmers who 
were infected by cowpox, a milder version of 
smallpox, were never plagued by the latter 
disease. As an experiment, he took pus from a 
milkmaid who had cowpox and scratched it 
into the arm of a small boy. After a six-week

valuable 
 
transmission = the disease 
being passed from one person 
to another 
 
outbreaks = sudden increases 
in a particular area 
 
stopping in their tracks = 
stopping something exactly 
where it is, so it can’t make 
any more progress 
 
antibodies = cells that fight 
disease 
 
mild = weak, little, not 
strong/intense 
 
full-fledged = the fully-
developed, complete version 
 
equipped = prepared and 
having the necessary resources

injury or skin problem 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
period, he then inoculated that small boy with the 
smallpox infection. When the boy did not get sick, 
Jenner continued his studies, which paved the 
way for the later work of Louis Pasteur—the man 
who developed the cholera and anthrax vaccines.  
 
Vaccines started to become part of standard 
medical treatment in the late nineteenth century, 
with the first laws obligating citizens to be 
vaccinated. The twentieth century saw the 
successful introduction of vaccines for many more 
diseases – including polio, which can cause muscle 
weakness and paralysis. Thanks to the vaccine, 
the number of polio cases in the U.S. dropped from 
35,000/year to under 200 within a mere ten years.  
 
While there is no scientific evidence that vaccines 
have any widespread negative side effects, a 
significant contingent of citizens have voiced 
concern in recent years. The controversy started 
with the publication of a study linking autism to 
childhood vaccinations. Although this research was 
later discredited, the damage had been done – 
parents with a deep-seated distrust of 
pharmaceutical companies began refusing to allow 
doctors to vaccinate their children.

Some “anti-vaxxers” are clamoring for an end to 
compulsory vaccinations. Currently, the United 
States requires children to be vaccinated in order 
to attend public school – although there are certain 
exemptions to this policy, including for medical, 
religious, and philosophical reasons. But with a 
significant number of parents opting out of 
vaccinations for their children, the country is now 
seeing a resurgence of diseases that vaccines had 
previously quelled. These diseases could be 
deadly for people who cannot be vaccinated 
themselves due to medical reasons, such as infants 
and those with compromised immune systems.  
 
Critics of compulsory vaccination believe that 
forcing parents to vaccinate their children is an 
infringement on their liberties. Defenders of 
compulsory vaccination contend that being 
vaccinated is a matter of safety and social 
responsibility.  
 
The Centers for Disease Control estimates that, 
between 1994 and 2014, the lives of 732,000 
American children were saved thanks to vaccines. 
The anti-vaxxers must ask themselves: is the one-
in-a-million chance of an adverse reaction really 
worth a return to the era when plagues decimated the population?

to a requirement

not to do something

made quiet

weakened or reduced

large part of

lessons.title: Stories Behind World Landmarks
lessons.fullText:
Stories Behind Famous  
World Landmarks 
 
Famous landmarks are magnets for tourists, 
artists, students, and lovers. We marvel at them, 
buy postcards, and take selfies so we can say 
we’ve been there. But how much do we know 
about their histories? Here are a few snapshots 
of the stories behind four famous sights.  
 
The Little Mermaid 
This small sculpture is perched on a rock by the 
seashore in Copenhagen, Denmark. Carl Jacobson 
commissioned sculptor Edvard Eriksen to craft 
this lovely bronze and granite statue as an 
homage to the mermaid in the fairy tale by 
Hans Christian Andersen. Jacobson, who had 
seen the fairy tale performed in a ballet, wanted 
to base the sculpture on the lead ballerina. 
However, she refused to model for the nude 
sculpture, so the mermaid’s face was based on 
the ballerina and her shapely body was based on 
Eriksen’s wife. Sadly, the Little Mermaid has 
been vandalized several times – including being 
decapitated – and the statue now on display is a 
replica. 
marvel at = be amazed or 
impressed by 
 
selfies = photos of oneself 
 
snapshots = quick summaries 
 
perched = sitting lightly (like a 
bird) 
 
craft = create with artistic skill 
 
homage = honor, recognition 
 
fairy tale = fictional story full 
of fantasy elements 
 
nude = naked (completely 
without clothes) 
 
shapely = having a pleasant 
shape 
 
decapitated = its head was 
cut off 
 
replica = copy of the original 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Sagrada Família 
One must-see when visiting Barcelona is the 
Sagrada Família, a Roman Catholic church that 
has been under construction for over a hundred 
years and remains incomplete. Its radical design 
was the brainchild of Antoni Gaudi, who came 
on board one year after the building began in 
1882. The construction, which is funded entirely 
by donations, has proceeded intermittently 
over the past century and is expected to be 
finished in 2026 to commemorate the 100th 
anniversary of Gaudi’s death. The design has 
been polarizing – some critics adore the 
unique, whimsical stonework and others decry 
it as one of the most bizarre and hideous 
buildings in the world.  
 
Rock of Gibraltar  
Not every landmark is manmade – the Rock of 
Gibraltar is one of the most majestic natural 
landmarks. It juts into the Mediterranean Sea at 
the southern tip of Europe; the ancient Greeks 
viewed it as “the end of the world.”  
 
must-see = a place or object 
that should be seen 
 
brainchild = idea or invention 
 
came on board = joined the 
project 
 
intermittently = stopping and 
starting, not continuous 
 
critics = people who analyze 
and evaluate art, literature, 
architecture, movies, etc. 
 
whimsical = playful 
 
decry = express disapproval of 
 
bizarre = strange (negative 
connotation) 
 
hideous = extremely ugly 
 
majestic = impressive in a 
dignified or inspiring way 
 
juts into = protrudes, extends 
into 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
One interesting feature of the Rock of 
Gibraltar is the 304-meter network of 
tunnels it contains. The British dug these 
tunnels in the late 1700s in order to defend 
the territory during a siege. 
 
Easter Island moai 
Nearly 900 giant stone statues, called moai, 
line the perimeter of this small South 
Pacific island. The statues were constructed 
over 800 years ago, and each weighs around 
13 tons. The faces depict the deified 
ancestors of the native people, gazing upon 
the villages as though they were guardians.  
 
The great enigma of the Easter Island 
statues is how they were brought from the 
quarry where they were carved to their 
locations on the coast. Researchers have 
attempted to replicate the feat by rolling 
the statues on top of logs. It is also possible 
that the statues were “walked” in an 
upright position with a rocking motion and 
an ingenious use of ropes. The island’s 
clans toppled the moai during the collapse 
of their civilization in the 18th and 19th 
centuries. 
siege = surrounding of an area by 
an attacking army that wants to 
capture it 
 
perimeter = outer edge of an area 
 
depict = show, display 
 
gazing = looking thoughtfully 
 
guardians = people responsible for 
protecting someone or something 
 
quarry = a place where stone is 
removed from the ground 
 
carved = form a shape or design by 
cutting 
 
feat = accomplishment 
 
upright = vertical 
 
rocking = a motion that goes from 
side to side 
 
ingenious = characterized by great 
skill, intelligence, and creativity 
 
clans = tribes or communities 
based on family relationships 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Comprehension Questions 
1. The Little Mermaid is located by... 
a. a lake 
b. a river 
c. the ocean 
2. The mermaid's body is based on... 
a. a ballerina 
b. a famous model 
c. the sculptor's wife 
3. The Sagrada Família is incomplete because... 
a. it has not yet been finished 
b. it was designed to be incomplete 
c. it was destroyed in a war 
4. The design can best be described as... 
a. futuristic 
b. traditional 
c. unusual 
5. The Rock of Gibraltar was viewed as "the end of the world" by the... 
a. British 
b. Greeks 
c. Romans 
6. The tunnels were created for... 
a. hiding persecuted people 
b. defensive military action 
c. mining for precious metals 
7. The statues on Easter Island are of... 
a. animals 
b. people 
c. religious symbols 
8. We still don’t know exactly how the Easter Island statues were... 
a. made 
b. destroyed 
c. transported 
 


 
 
Discover New Words 
 
Choose the best definition for the vocabulary word in bold. 
 
1. Famous landmarks are magnets for tourists, artists, students, and lovers. 
a. are created by 
b. attract a lot of 
c. are fun for 
 
2. Sadly, the Little Mermaid has been vandalized several times – including 
being decapitated – and the statue now on display is a replica. 
a. criticized in the media 
b. damaged on purpose 
c. stolen or removed 
 
3. The design has been polarizing – some critics adore the unique, whimsical 
stonework and others decry it as one of the most bizarre and hideous 
buildings in the world. 
a. causing opinions to be divided 
b. inspiring to others 
c. totally unique 
 
4. The great enigma of the Easter Island statues is how they were brought from 
the quarry where they were carved to their locations on the coast.  
a. discovery 
b. importance 
c. mystery 
 
5. The island’s clans toppled the moai during the collapse of their civilization in 
the 18th and 19th centuries.  
a. built slowly over many years 
b. knocked down; hit and caused to fall 
c. worshipped as gods

lessons.title: World's Most Expensive Foods
lessons.fullText:
The World’s Most Expensive Foods 
If you could spend an unlimited amount of money 
on something delicious to eat, what would you 
choose? If you have money to burn, you might 
like to pick out one of the world’s most expensive 
foods. Which one of these pleases your palate? 
Bagels 
For a thousand dollars, the chef of the Westin 
Hotel in New York will present you with a 
delicately toasted bagel, topped with goji berry 
and white truffle cream cheese, infused with a 
jelly made from Riesling wine. What makes it so 
expensive? It’s the truffles – white truffles are the 
most expensive in the world. They grow only in 
Alba, Italy, under certain oak trees. 
Potatoes 
Would you believe that potatoes could cost $45 
per pound? It’s true. The La Bonnotte potato only 
grows on a particular French island. It has to be 
harvested by hand, and the growing season is a 
mere ten days in the month of May. You can buy 
it only in the ritziest restaurants in the 
Netherlands and France. 
money to burn = a LOT of 
extra money, much more 
than you need 
palate = sense of taste 
toasted = describes a 
piece of bread that is 
heated and turned brown 
by bringing it close to a 
fire or heat source 
white truffle = a very 
expensive type of fungus 
infused with = filled with 
harvested = when a fruit 
or vegetable is gathered 
from the place where it is 
growing 
a mere ten days = only ten 
days (the word “mere” is 
used for emphasis when a 
quantity is small) 
 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Mushrooms 
You won’t find matsutake mushrooms in your 
local supermarket. They’re found only in Japan, 
only in autumn, and they can’t be cultivated. The 
trees under which they grow are becoming 
scarce, and these mushrooms cost in the 
neighborhood of a thousand dollars for a pound. 
Frittata 
Another thousand-dollar dish is the breakfast 
frittata that upscale restaurants create using the 
world’s third-most expensive variety of caviar – 
ten ounces of it, at a cost to the restaurant of $65 
per ounce – combined with lobster and, of course, 
eggs. 
Samundari Khazana Curry 
For $3,200, you can dine on the most expensive 
curry in the world, available from Bombay 
Brassiere. It consists of white truffle, Devon crab, 
beluga caviar and half a tomato, garnished in 
gold leaf. Add to that a Scottish lobster (also 
coated in gold), quail eggs stuffed with caviar, 
and abalone, and you have a dish fit for a king… 
and it’s likely that only a king can afford it! 
 
cultivated = grown and 
produced deliberately by 
humans 
in the neighborhood of = 
approximately 
upscale = high-level, fancy, 
expensive 
caviar = fish eggs 
dine on = eat (the word 
“dine” is like a more 
refined word for eat) 
coated in = covered in 
abalone = a type of 
shellfish 
fit for a king = very fancy; 
appropriate for a king 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Wagyu Steak 
Japanese Wagyu cattle are fed beer and 
massaged by hand to ensure the superior 
marbling and tenderness of the meat. The fat 
content is through the roof, so people at risk for 
heart problems should likely avoid it.  
If you’re in good health, though, and want to taste 
a steak from the world’s most pampered cow, 
you can get a Wagyu steak at Craftsteak in New 
York for just $2,800.  
Pizza Royale 007  
You’d think that $4,200 would get you more than 
just a twelve-inch pie, but not when it’s topped 
with cognac-marinated lobster, champagne-
soaked caviar, smoked salmon from Scotland, 
venison, and the finest prosciutto.  
Add to that a garnish of 24-carat gold flakes, and 
you have the world’s most expensive pizza. 
Yubari Melons 
If you think something as simple as a piece of 
fruit couldn’t possibly be expensive – think again! 
The most expensive melons ever sold were a pair 
of Yubari cantaloupes that were grown in 2008.  
At auction, they fetched $22,872 – that’s 
cattle = cows 
massaged = rubbing and 
pressing the body with the 
hands 
marbling = the mixture of 
fat and muscle in the meat 
tenderness = softness, 
easy to chew 
cognac-marinated = 
cognac is a type of liquor, 
and “marinate” means to 
soak meat in a liquid, so 
that the liquid affects the 
flavor of the meat

deer 
prosciutto = a type of 
Italian ham 
flakes = tiny, thin pieces 
auction = an event where 
potential buyers say how 
much they are willing to 
pay for the item, until the 
person who offers the 
highest price wins and 
buys it

Vocabulary 


 
 
$11,436 per melon. You should never again 
complain about your grocery bill. 
The Golden Opulence Sundae 
Time for dessert – it’ll run you about $1,000. The 
Golden Opulence Sundae is made from Tahitian 
vanilla ice cream topped with chocolate syrup 
made from melting one of the world’s most 
expensive chocolates. The sundae is also 
adorned with caviar, exotic candied fruit, 
truffles, marzipan cherries, and edible 23-carat 
gold leaf.  
After meals like these, your stomach will be full, 
but your wallet will be lighter! 
Sources: 
http://most-expensive.com/foods  
http://www.urbanspoon.com/articles/13059/

the dish

liquid

turns into a liquid

with; made beautiful with

of money

lessons.title: Young Entrepreneurs
lessons.fullText:
Young Entrepreneurs 
 
Most people spend their youth learning, growing, 
and goofing off. A select few, however, manage 
to turn their childhood into a staging ground for 
future accomplishments. Here are three people 
who started successful companies before they 
were 18 years old. 
 
David Buckingham:  
Custom Alaskan Outhouses 
 
Who would think there’s a market for outhouses 
in the 21st century? Talk about a tiny niche! Yet 
an industrious 16-year-old named David 
Buckingham started building and selling 
customized outhouses in Alaska.   
 
Most people buy the outhouses for their 
aesthetic appeal rather than their functionality, 
since most Alaskan homes do in fact have indoor 
plumbing and running water. But David was still 
able to tap into a niche market of people looking 
for the authentic rustic feel of an outhouse built 
to their exact specifications. 
 
goofing off = being silly 
staging ground = 
preparation 
outhouses = outdoor 
bathrooms / toilets that 
are in a small building 
separate from the main 
house 
niche = small, specialized 
area of the market 
aesthetic appeal = the 
attractive way they look 
plumbing = the system of 
pipes and water inside a 
house or building 
tap into = access an area 
of resources 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Aaron Swartz:  
Co-creator of RSS 1.0 and Reddit 
 
RSS is a computer program that aggregates 
posts from a number of different compatible 
sources; such as blogs, twitter feeds, and 
article headlines. If a website has a live-
streaming update of posts or other data, it 
probably uses RSS.  
 
Aaron Swartz co-authored RSS 1.0 when he 
was just 14. He went on to form his own 
company, Infogami, and was later involved in 
the creation of the popular social media site 
Reddit. As an adult, Aaron was an outspoken 
activist, particularly supporting government 
transparency and the early stages of net 
neutrality.  
 
Sadly, Aaron took things too far in his quest 
to make information freely available. He 
broke into a university building to install a 
computer to secretly download articles from 
a digital academic library with paid access. In 
the midst of Aaron’s trial, he took his own 
life. 
 
aggregates = brings together 
compatible = things that can 
work well together 
live-streaming = appearing at 
the same time as the content 
is produced 
co-authored = wrote together 
with other people 
activist = someone who 
supports and works in favor of 
a particular cause 
transparency = being clear 
and not hiding anything 
net neutrality = the principle 
that all internet data should 
be treated as equal, not 
restricted by governments or 
companies 
took things too far = went 
beyond what is acceptable 
broke into = illegally entered a 
building or house 
took his own life = committed 
suicide; killed himself 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Anshul Samar:  
Alchemist Empire Inc. 
 
When Anshul was in 4th grade, he played a lot of 
card games – and then decided that he'd like to 
make his own. Two years later, he released the 
first version of his game, Elementeo, which is a 
card game geared towards kids and based on 
the periodic table of the elements. Anshul then 
went on to found Alchemist Empire Inc., a 
company that manages the production and 
marketing of Elementeo. The game has earned 
extensive media coverage, and it was also 
presented at the National Academies of Sciences 
and the American Chemical Society. Anshul 
Samar is now a freshman at Stanford University 
and still runs Elementeo as its founder and CEO.
